wrapTickLabel = (label, maxWidth = 10) => {
  if (!label || label.length <= maxWidth) return label;
  const words = label.split(" ");
  const lines = [];
  let currentLine = "";
  for (const word of words) {
    if ((currentLine + " " + word).trim().length <= maxWidth) {
      currentLine = (currentLine + " " + word).trim();
    } else {
      if (currentLine) lines.push(currentLine);
      currentLine = word;
    }
  }
  if (currentLine) lines.push(currentLine);
  return lines.join("\n");
}

START HERE • USER GUIDE & PHYSICAL TELECONNECTIONS

Section 0 • How to Use the Kenya ENSO Explorer

An empirical climate intelligence and decision-support system linking large-scale equatorial ocean dynamics (Pacific ENSO, Indian Ocean Dipole, and Western Pacific Gradient) to county-level agricultural production, rangeland forage resilience, flood inundation, and humanitarian emergency vulnerability across Kenya's 47 counties.

Statutory Authority & Forecast Boundary: The ENSO Explorer is an empirical research and risk assessment platform designed for climate rationale development, long-term contingency planning, and adaptation financing. It is NOT an operational daily weather forecast or statutory seasonal warning. For official, binding meteorological advisories and early warnings in Kenya, consult the statutory authority: the Kenya Meteorological Service Authority (KMSA; formerly KMD) under the Meteorology Act No. 7 of 2026 at meteo.go.ke and the IGAD Climate Prediction & Applications Centre (ICPAC) at icpac.net.
Loading Executive County Climate Brief & 2-Page Anticipatory Action Matrix…

Three-Step Decision Workflow for County Officials & Proposal Writers

Follow this structured path to translate planetary climate signals into actionable county investment priorities and defensible adaptation finance rationales (GCF, AF, GEF, CIDP).

1

Select County & Season

Use the sticky control toolbar above to choose your target county and primary agricultural season (OND Short Rains or MAM Long Rains). Inspect Section 1 to review official KNBS crop and livestock baselines, modeled production value, and multi-dimensional vulnerability rankings.

2

Inspect Seasonal Outlook

Check the live NOAA CPC equatorial ocean state probabilities and view the top historical analogue seasons ranked by Euclidean distance in joint ocean-temperature space. Examine empirical tercile shifts and multi-hazard outcomes from the most similar historical seasons.

3

Review Historical Evidence

Examine 44-year CHIRPS rainfall distributions, satellite raster history (NDVI, SAR flood, WRSI), and audited KNBS harvest shocks across past ocean states. Build empirical causal baselines that satisfy donor review standards without relying on ungrounded assumptions.

Understanding Kenya's Planetary Teleconnections in Plain Language

Kenya's bimodal rainfall is governed by three distinct ocean and atmospheric teleconnection engines operating across thousands of miles of tropical ocean.

ENSO (Pacific Ocean)

RONI Index

El Niño–Southern Oscillation: The warming (El Niño) and cooling (La Niña) of surface waters across the central-eastern equatorial Pacific. In Kenya, El Niño shifts the atmospheric Walker circulation, strongly favoring above-normal rainfall during the OND Short Rains (flood risk), whereas La Niña strongly favors severe drought.

Governing metric: Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI)

IOD (Indian Ocean)

DMI Index

Indian Ocean Dipole: An east-west temperature see-saw across the equatorial Indian Ocean. A Positive IOD (+IOD) warms the western Indian Ocean near Kenya, pumping vast moisture inland. When a +IOD co-occurs with El Niño (as in 1997, 2006, and 2023)—or occurs as an extreme standalone event during ENSO-neutral conditions (as in 2019)—it causes historic mega-floods. Negative IOD (-IOD) exacerbates drought.

Governing metric: Dipole Mode Index (DMI)

Western-V (Western Pacific)

WNP Metric

Western Pacific Gradient: A sea-surface temperature and convective gradient across the Western North Pacific that drives East Africa's MAM Long Rains. During MAM, canonical Pacific ENSO correlations decouple across Kenya, and the Western-V mode takes precedence in modulating monsoon onset and moisture transport.

Governing metric: Western North Pacific anomaly (WNP)
Spatial & Seasonal Regime Notice: Why "One Rule for Kenya" Fails

While El Niño brings surplus moisture to northern pastoral ASALs (Marsabit, Wajir, Garissa) and eastern lowlands during OND, western Kenya (Lake Victoria basin, Trans Nzoia, Uasin Gishu) follows a distinct rainfall regime with substantial June–August (JJA) rainfall governed by Congo moisture fluxes. Always examine county-specific climatology (Section 1) rather than applying national generalizations.

Data Sources & Administrative Framework

Geographic land area, population headcounts, and administrative ward boundaries are established under the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) 2019 Kenya Population & Housing Census (Volume I, Volume II & Volume IV) and the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) official gazette.

Boundary Universes & Sub-County Nomenclature

IEBC Electoral Constituencies vs. KNBS Administrative Sub-Counties: The 290 sub-county units mapped across this atlas represent official IEBC parliamentary constituencies (standardized as UN OCHA COD-AB Level 2 boundaries). In national statistical reporting, KNBS designates 345 administrative sub-counties. In certain counties, these universes diverge: for instance, Marsabit comprises 4 electoral constituencies (Laisamis, Moyale, North Horr, and Saku) corresponding to 7 KNBS administrative sub-counties. Both spatial definitions are administratively recognized; however, because KNBS does not publish polygon geometries for the 345 administrative sub-counties, all high-resolution spatial overlays in this explorer utilize the authoritative 290 IEBC constituency boundaries.

Population Re-Levelling & Spatial Disaggregation
  • KNBS County Level Re-Levelling: Raw unconstrained WorldPop raster sums nationally total ~55.1 million, exceeding Kenya's 2019 census population (47.56 million). All population totals in this atlas are rigorously re-levelled to official KNBS county totals (2019 Census headcount and 2026 KNBS projections).
  • Within-County Spatial Distribution: Population headcounts are distributed across constituencies using WorldPop 100 m constrained residential building footprint shares. Within each county, constituency shares are anchored to the 2020 baseline distribution, while county growth rates track official KNBS demographic projections.
  • Dominant Season Derivation & Equimodal Regimes: Seasonality classification is derived from the 30-year CHIRPS v3 (1991–2020) WMO climatological baseline. Sub-counties are classified into three distinct physical rainfall regimes:
    • Bimodal (Equimodal): Where MAM and OND seasonal accumulations differ by less than 25 mm or each season accounts for 45%–55% of the total bimodal volume (e.g. Saku in Marsabit: 289.7 mm MAM vs. 279.0 mm OND, 50.9% vs. 49.1%). In these balanced transition zones, neither season overwhelms the other, and pastoral forage replenishment depends critically on both rainfall windows.
    • MAM (Long Rains): Where MAM accounts for >55% of bimodal rainfall and exceeds OND by at least 25 mm (characteristic of western Kenya, central highlands, and Rift Valley).
    • OND (Short Rains): Where OND accounts for >55% of bimodal rainfall and exceeds MAM by at least 25 mm (characteristic of eastern pastoral lowlands including Garissa, Wajir, Mandera, and Tana River).
  • Proposal & Finance Alignment: County demographics and surface area figures align directly with the Commission on Revenue Allocation (CRA) Third Basis for Revenue Sharing formula and County Integrated Development Plans (CIDPs).

Data Sources & Ingestion Pipeline

Official county production statistics are extracted from the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) National Agricultural Produce Reports (NAPR 2019–2024 editions), Agriculture and Food Authority (AFA) rice statistics, and the 2019 Kenya Population & Housing Census Volume IV (Distribution of Population by Socio-Economic Characteristics).

Audit Trail & Reconciliation Protocol
  • Dual-Engine Extraction: Official published report tables were extracted via dual PDF table engines (PyMuPDF and pdfplumber) with character-level coordinate verification and automated OCR cross-checks.
  • National Additivity Reconciliation: For every crop and livestock species, sub-national county values are audited against published national totals to ensure the sum of counties equals the published national figure within ±0.05% rounding tolerance.
  • Crucial Protocol: Blank ≠ Zero: An unsurveyed county or commodity in a specific reporting cycle is coded as missing (NaN / ∅ marker), NOT zero. A reported zero denotes an active survey recording zero yield. For arid rangeland counties (e.g., Marsabit, Turkana), rainfed crop farming is concentrated in isolated agro-pastoral sub-counties (e.g. Mount Marsabit / Saku); missing years reflect non-surveyed cycles rather than complete crop failure.
  • Administrative Statistics Baseline: These official statistics published by KNBS provide the recognized administrative baseline for county planning (CIDP) and project design documentation.

Figure 1.2

Spatially Modeled Value of Production Portfolio (IFPRI MapSPAM & FAO GLW4) — Marsabit

Gross agricultural capital portfolio in nominal 2021 USD (vop_nominal-usd21; undeflated) modeled via IFPRI MapSPAM (1 km crops) and FAO GLW4 (1 km livestock).

Methodological Boundary & Valuation Caveats: MapSPAM and GLW4 provide downscaled econometric distributions expressed on a Nominal 2021 USD basis (vop_nominal-usd21; undeflated). Because values are undeflated, cross-timeframe comparisons conflate macroeconomic price inflation with physical hazard shifts. While downscaled using global spatial priors, both layers are anchored to national agricultural census baselines (IFPRI MapSPAM 2020 v1r2 and FAO GLW4 2020, valued at 2019–23 national farm-gate prices: FAOSTAT’s implied price with cited corrections, method in hazards_prototype/docs/methods/nominal_price_method.md), so national totals align with FAOSTAT (livestock reconciles at 1.00 since the September 2026 republication, hazards_prototype#30). Species Scope (Exclusion of Camels): FAO GLW4 maps cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, and poultry, but excludes camels. In camel-pastoral northern ASALs (Marsabit, Wajir, Mandera, Garissa), modeled livestock capital represents ruminants and poultry only; total pastoral wealth is substantially higher when including camel herds (see Section 1.1 for official KNBS census numbers). These modeled totals remain essential for demonstrating to international donors that livestock represents 90%–97% of agricultural wealth in pastoral ASALs (directing adaptation finance proportionally to pastoral resilience while safeguarding vital highland agro-pastoral cropping sanctuaries like Saku and Moyale). However, because they are modeled from global priors, they must not be cited as subcounty administrative census statistics. Use Section 1.1 for legal administrative census numbers.
Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)
Data Sources & Modeling Prior

Crop capital distributions are modeled from the IFPRI Spatial Production Allocation Model (MapSPAM 2020 v1r2) at 1 km resolution. Livestock capital distributions are downscaled from the FAO Gridded Livestock of the World (GLW4) at 1 km resolution, disaggregated across cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, and poultry. Note: FAO GLW4 does not model camels, an indispensable pastoral capital asset in northern ASALs (see Section 1.1 for official KNBS camel census counts).

Econometric Normalization & Scope
  • Nominal Currency Basis (vop_nominal-usd21): All production outputs and herd headcounts are monetized into Nominal 2021 USD (undeflated) at 2019–23 national farm-gate prices (crops: FAOSTAT’s implied price with producer-price fallback and cited evidence pins; livestock: FAOSTAT producer prices). Because this series is undeflated, multi-year comparisons mix macroeconomic price inflation with climate hazard shifts.
  • Price Method Update (2026-10-06): The upstream exposure tables were republished with a revised nominal price method (hazards_prototype#38–40); the livestock reconciliation defect (hazards_prototype#30) was resolved in September 2026. The hazard-exposure layer was re-baked on the same prices the same day, so exposed-value shares are consistent with these totals (Kenya robusta coffee excepted: one Lake Victoria border cell is attributed to Uganda in the hazard layer).
  • Spatial Zonal Aggregation: 1 km grid cells are zonal-summed over official Kenya county boundary vectors to establish gross agricultural capital endowments.
  • Spatial Nuance: In arid rangelands (e.g., Marsabit, Turkana, Wajir, Mandera), rainfed field cropping is not uniformly spread; it is clustered in highland agro-pastoral pockets (e.g. Saku and Moyale in Marsabit) or irrigated river corridors.
  • Strategic Financing Role: In pastoral ASAL counties, pastoralist herds represent 90%–97% of agricultural Value of Production (VoP). This establishes the macroeconomic evidence required by GCF and Adaptation Fund investment boards to prioritize rangeland water retention, index-based livestock insurance (IBLI), and veterinary cold chains over unviable crop irrigation schemes.

Why this data & analysis? Official Baseline

The "Best Available Data" Reality: Climate project proposals (GCF, GEF, Adaptation Fund) frequently fail donor review because they rely on modelled or unverified third-party socio-economic indicators. We exclusively use the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) 2019 National Population & Housing Census and 2023 County Gender Data Sheets. These are Kenya's official national statistics used by the Commission on Revenue Allocation (CRA).

Key Assumptions
  • Structural Baseline: Multi-dimensional poverty headcounts and household structures are assumed to represent decadal vulnerability baselines that exacerbate climate shock sensitivity.
  • Census Coverage: County totals are pegged directly to the official KNBS census gazetteer, with 100% additivity across all 47 counties.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Inter-Censal Drifts: Changes occurring post-2019 (e.g., population displacement following the 2020–2023 drought) are not reflected in static census tables.
  • Intra-County Heterogeneity: County-level averages mask acute disparities between urban county headquarters (e.g. Saku) and remote pastoral wards (e.g. North Horr).
Primary Source: KNBS 2019 Census • KNBS 2023 County Gender Data Sheets • data/KE-enso-explorer/gesi_v2.parquet

2 • Outlook & Scenario Preparedness

Section 2 • Seasonal Outlook & Preparedness — Marsabit

Live ocean driver telemetry, official KMSA/NOAA seasonal projections, and nearest historical analogue preparedness scenarios.

Operational Purpose: This section equips county directors, disaster risk committees, and development partners to anchor anticipatory action in empirical physical evidence. It supports pre-season contingency budgeting, seed distribution (drought-tolerant cereals vs waterlogging-tolerant varieties), livestock disease ring-vaccination, and borehole/culvert clearing before seasonal rains commence.
The Three-Tier Early Warning Architecture:
1. Ocean Teleconnection Forcing
Global equatorial Pacific (RONI) and Indian Ocean Dipole (DMI) sea surface temperature configurations. Sets planetary boundary conditions; does not constitute a localized rainfall forecast.
2. Seasonal Rainfall Outlook
Empirical tercile probability distributions conditioned on matched historical analogues (Figure 2.1). Official seasonal forecasts and 7-day county advisories are legally issued exclusively by KMSA.
3. Forward Impact Scenarios
End-to-end historical analogue scenarios (Figure 2.2) demonstrating how multi-hazard shocks (crop deficits, pasture crashes, floods, and market Terms of Trade deterioration) propagated during matched ocean years.
Official Governance & Statutory Alignment

Kenya Meteorological Service Authority (KMSA) Statutory Framework

Pursuant to the Meteorology Act No. 7 of 2026 (assented March 13, 2026), the Kenya Meteorological Service Authority (KMSA; official products may retain Kenya Meteorological Department/KMD branding during transition) is the statutory designated authority legally mandated to formulate, issue, and regulate all official weather forecasts, seasonal climate outlooks, and operational early warning advisories in the Republic of Kenya.

Mandate Boundary & Platform Role: The Adaptation Atlas does not produce independent operational forecasts or issue unilateral disaster directives. It provides historical analogue scenarios and teleconnection risk diagnostics. County governments, disaster committees, and development partners must strictly anchor all operational triggers and contingency funding to official KMSA bulletins and localized advisories from County Directors of Meteorology (CDMs).

Why this analogue method? Empirical Conditioning

The "Best Available Data" Reality: Dynamic numerical climate models often exhibit systematic rainfall biases over East Africa's complex terrain. Evaluating empirical historical analogues with matched equatorial Pacific (RONI) and Indian Ocean (DMI) sea surface temperature configurations grounds scenarios in observed physical reality.

Key Assumptions
  • Standardized Metric Space: Standardized by empirical 1991–2020 baseline standard deviations across pre-season and concurrent peak windows (σRONI ≈ 0.74–1.12 °C, σDMI ≈ 0.37 °C) to prevent higher Pacific variance (~4× to 9× variance ratio) from dominating the Indian Ocean Dipole.
  • Tropical-Mean Background Subtraction: NOAA CPC Relative ONI (RONI) removes global tropical mean SST anomalies month-by-month and rescales variance to isolate atmospheric Walker circulation contrast from secular warming.
Caveats & Limitations
  • No Two Events Are Identical: Atmospheric noise and Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) intra-seasonal pulses can modulate outcomes.
  • KMSA Operational Precedence: Statutory operational planning requires official KMSA seasonal forecast confirmation.
Primary Source: NOAA CPC ERSSTv6 • NOAA CPC / HadISST DMI • CHIRPS v3
MAM Teleconnection

Long Rains (MAM) Boundary & Western-V Dynamics

Why Pacific ENSO forecasts have near-zero skill for March–May in Kenya.

A common institutional mistake is applying El Niño or La Niña forecasts to Kenya's Long Rains (MAM). In equatorial East Africa, Pacific ENSO skill drops close to zero during the boreal spring predictability barrier:

Physical Mechanisms Driving MAM Rainfall:
  • The Western-V SST Gradient: Differential warming between the western Pacific and Indian Ocean steers localized subsidence over Kenya (Funk et al., 2019).
  • Regional Air-Sea Interaction: Localized moisture convergence from the Congo Basin and southwestern Indian Ocean dominates over distant ENSO signals.
  • Operational Guidance: For MAM planning, county directors must consult KMSA downscaled March–May outlooks rather than global ENSO news trackers.

Why Analogue Multi-Hazard Diagnostics? Empirical Grounding

Single-variable rainfall forecasts fail to capture compound hazard transmission. By coupling historical ocean states with satellite-derived pasture vegetative flushes (MODIS NDVI) and pastoral grain exchange rates (FEWS NET/NDMA Terms of Trade), county directors can evaluate how previous analogous seasons impacted food security, livestock markets, and emergency response budgets.

Key Assumptions
  • Standardized Predictor Space: Nearest neighbours are ranked using normalized Euclidean distance in joint RONI + DMI space.
  • Two-Season Memory: Pasture and livestock conditions depend heavily on whether the preceding MAM Long Rains were wet or dry.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Market Context: Terms of trade reflect historical commodity price regimes and macro inflation that may differ from current economic baselines.
  • Local Variations: Micro-climates and intra-seasonal dry spells can modulate local outcomes even in wet analogue years.
Primary Source: NOAA CPC ERSSTv6 • CHIRPS v3 • MODIS NDVI • NDMA / FEWS NET
Official Government Guidance Statutory Mandate: Meteorology Act No. 7 of 2026 (Republic of Kenya)

Official Kenya Meteorological Service Authority (KMSA) Seasonal Sectoral Advisory Matrix

Synthesized from official seasonal sectoral guidance frameworks issued by the Kenya Meteorological Service Authority (KMSA) (formerly KMD) in liaison with the Ministry of Agriculture & Livestock Development, Ministry of Water, Sanitation & Irrigation, National Drought Management Authority (NDMA), and Kenya Red Cross Society (KRCS).

meteo.go.ke Seasonal Forecasts → meteo.go.ke CAP Weather Warnings → meteo.go.ke National Portal →
Release Cadence & Operational Sourcing: Sourced directly from official seasonal releases: The October–November–December (OND) Seasonal Climate Outlook and Potential Socio-Economic Impacts (Ref: KMD/FCST/SO Series) and The March–April–May (MAM) Seasonal Climate Outlook. Bulletins are published bi-annually (late August / early September for OND Short Rains; late February for MAM Long Rains). County-specific operational actions are regulated by downscaled 7-day weather advisories issued directly by County Directors of Meteorology (CDMs).
Agriculture & Food Security

Crop Production & Post-Harvest Advisory

  • Certified Drought-Tolerant Seeds: Promote dryland cereals (sorghum, finger millet) and pulses (green grams, cowpeas, dolichos lablab) certified by KALRO and state agricultural offices.
  • Moisture Conservation: Deploy in-situ rainwater harvesting techniques including zai pits, tied ridges, and stone contour bunds across agro-pastoral zones.
  • Post-Harvest Protection: If above-normal rains extend into harvest periods, mobilize hermetic storage bags and mobile grain dryers to prevent post-harvest mold and aflatoxin contamination.
Source: KMSA Seasonal Advisory Guidelines (Agriculture Sector) • Ministry of Agriculture & Livestock Development
Pastoralism & Livestock

Rangeland & Animal Health Advisory

  • Strategic Pasture Grazing Reserves: Demarcate dry-season grazing areas and establish fodder banks (hay baling, reseeding of denuded rangelands) ahead of dry spells.
  • Epizootic Disease Surveillance: Flood conditions following severe drought trigger acute outbreaks of mosquito-borne Rift Valley Fever (RVF) and Contagious Caprine Pleuropneumonia (CCPP). Pre-position ring-vaccination doses.
  • Strategic Commercial De-stocking: During developing drought phases, trigger commercial offtake before animal body condition deteriorates below market exchange thresholds.
Source: KMSA Pastoral Advisory Matrix • Directorate of Veterinary Services • NDMA
Water & Sanitation

Water Infrastructure & Quality Management

  • Dam & Pan Desilting: Desilt earth dams and municipal water pans prior to seasonal rains to maximize volumetric surface capture.
  • Borehole Protection & Water Treatment: Raise borehole wellhead aprons above historical flood lines. Stock community distribution centres with chlorine powder and household water purification sachets.
  • Flood Spillway Reinforcement: Inspect spillways of community water storage structures to prevent breach during high-intensity flash-flood events.
Source: KMSA Water Advisory Protocol • Ministry of Water, Sanitation & Irrigation
Disaster Risk Management

Emergency Contingency & Transport Access

  • Transport Drainage & Culvert Clearing: Clear seasonal storm runoff culverts along primary road corridors and feeder roads before onset to prevent transport severance.
  • County Committee Activation: Convene the County Disaster Risk Management Committee (CDRMC) under the National Disaster Risk Management Act, 2026 (Act No. 16 of 2026), co-chaired by the County Governor and County Commissioner upon KMSA alert issuance.
  • Community Early Warning: Transmit CDM downscaled advisories in local pastoral languages via vernacular FM radio and NDMA community channels.
Source: KMSA DRM Early Warning Protocols • NDMA Standard Operating Procedures

3 Historical Climate Evidence • 3.1 Climate Graphs

Section 3.1 • Climate Graphs & Empirical Contingency Distributions — Marsabit

Multi-decadal seasonal precipitation climatology, SPEI-3 drought anomalies, and ocean driver contingency distributions.

🧭 How to Navigate Historical Climate Evidence & Teleconnection Strength

Section 3 provides the empirical bedrock for county climate risk planning. Rather than relying solely on global climate model forecasts, this section catalogs what has actually happened across 44 years of satellite and ocean observations (1981–2024).

1. Questions Answered:
  • How dependable is the ENSO / IOD teleconnection in this specific county?
  • What are the empirical odds of a Wetter vs. Drier season during an El Niño or +IOD?
  • Which sub-counties face severe 100-year riverine flood exposure?
2. Reading Sequence:
  1. Fig 3.1: Multi-decadal rainfall & SPEI-3 anomaly history.
  2. Fig 3.2: Empirical contingency probabilities (tercile odds).
  3. Fig 3.3: Candidate driver regression & correlation ranking.
  4. Fig 3.4 & 3.5: High-resolution spatial raster grids & flood exposure.
3. Physical Limits & Caveats:
  • Non-stationarity: Past frequencies may shift under greenhouse warming.
  • Orographic satellite underestimation around isolated mountain massifs.
  • SAR blindspots: Sentinel-1 orbital passes miss brief flash flood events.
Figure 3.1

Multi-Decadal Precipitation Climatology & Standardized Anomalies (CHIRPS v3 & SPEI-3)

Historical seasonal rainfall and SPEI-3 anomaly time series (1981–2024) with ocean teleconnection markers.

Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)
Why this data & analysis? Spatial Continuity Rationale

The "Best Available Data" Reality: Ground-based meteorological stations in northern Kenya are extremely sparse—often fewer than one active, reliable rain gauge per 20,000 km². Relying purely on physical weather stations creates massive blind spots across ASAL pastoral rangelands. CHIRPS v3 (UCSB/CHC) blends cold-cloud duration satellite infrared with reporting stations to create continuous 5 km grids spanning 1981 to present. Satellite-gauge blending is the physically grounded standard to track pixel-level subcounty drought and flood anomalies continuously across Kenya.

Key Assumptions
  • WMO Climatological Baseline: Anomalies are computed against the 1991–2020 normal period (30 years) to conform to WMO standard reference rules.
  • Linear Detrending: Long-term greenhouse gas warming trends are detrended before calculating ENSO/IOD teleconnection correlations to isolate interannual ocean forcing.
  • Fixed Accumulation Windows: OND (Oct 1 – Dec 31) and MAM (Mar 1 – May 31) are treated as rigid seasonal boundaries matching agricultural calendars.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Orographic Underestimation: Thermal infrared satellite estimates systematically underestimate localized orographic rainfall around isolated mountain massifs (e.g. Mt. Marsabit, Mt. Kulal).
  • SPEI Evapotranspiration: SPEI-3 utilizes Hargreaves-Samani PET, which can over-estimate evaporative demand during hyper-thermal arid spells.
Primary Source: CHIRPS v3 (0.05°) • Vicente-Serrano SPEI-3 • s3://digital-atlas/domain=climate/type=precipitation/source=chirps-v3/
Figure 3.1B

Consecutive Seasonal Rainfall Sequences & Compounding Drought Runs (1982–2025)

Sequential evaluation of compound multi-season drought risk across consecutive production years (OND(Y−1) → MAM(Y)) and unbroken runs of sub-normal rainfall.

How to Read the Sequence View: Production year Y pairs the preceding Short Rains (OND of year Y−1) with the following Long Rains (MAM of year Y), matching the KNBS production-year convention where both harvests land within year Y. Each season is standardized independently against its own 1991–2020 WMO climatological baseline (never pooled). Cells are colored by standardized anomaly (z): Dry (z < −0.5, red), Normal (−0.5 ≤ z ≤ +0.5, gray), and Wet (z > +0.5, blue). Double failure years (dry / dry) are flagged distinctly as compounding multi-season drought emergencies. The run-length bar tracks unbroken consecutive seasons of sub-normal rainfall.
Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)
Why this data & analysis? Sequential Compounding Rationale

Sequences Matter More Than Averages: In East African bimodal climate regimes, single-season climate shocks can often be absorbed by household food reserves, pastoral herd condition, or regional grain trade. However, consecutive failures across both seasons trigger systemic collapse: rangeland forage deficits compound, livestock mortality accelerates, and rainfed staple harvests fail back-to-back. Averaging seasonal totals (such as OND+MAM) obscures this physical reality—a wet season and a catastrophic drought average out to "near-normal," hiding critical humanitarian risk. Evaluating the chronological sequence OND(Y−1) → MAM(Y) preserves the true multi-season shock trajectory.

Key Assumptions
  • KNBS Production Year Pairing: Year Y pairs the preceding Short Rains OND(Y−1) with Long Rains MAM(Y). Both harvests occur within calendar year Y, matching national agricultural accounting (KNBS NAPR) and HarvestStat Africa planted-year conventions.
  • Independent Seasonal Moments: OND and MAM are standardized separately against their own 1991–2020 normal period (WMO standard). The distributions have different means and variances and are never pooled.
  • Categorical Thresholds: Consistent with standard meteorological tercile definitions: Dry (z < −0.5), Wet (z > +0.5), and Near-normal (−0.5 ≤ z ≤ +0.5).
  • Unbroken Pastoral Stress Runs: Cumulative run length walks seasons in true chronological order (…OND(Y−1), MAM(Y), OND(Y), MAM(Y+1)…) counting unbroken consecutive sub-normal seasons (z < −0.5). Forage depletion compounds across seasons and does not reset at the calendar year.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Calendar Variations in 4 Counties: The production-year pairing convention (OND(Y−1) + MAM(Y)) is standard across 43 counties but knowingly differs in 4 counties where the cropping calendar is unimodal or has alternate planting regimes (project_season_year_convention).
  • Microclimatic Aggregation: County-level spatial averages blend agro-ecological zones; localized pastoral rangelands may experience multi-season drought even when high-elevation agricultural belts register near-normal rainfall.
  • Gaps vs. Zeros: Missing seasons are preserved as explicit gaps and never imputed as zero rainfall or normal conditions.
Primary Source: CHIRPS v3 (0.05°) • HarvestStat Africa • KNBS NAPR • s3://digital-atlas/domain=climate/type=precipitation/source=chirps-v3/
Figure 3.2

Empirical Contingency Probability Matrix (Tercile Likelihood given Ocean Driver Strength)

Observed conditional probabilities of Wetter, Near-normal, or Drier seasons conditioned on ENSO, IOD, and Western-V intensity classes (1981–2024 record).

How to Read Tercile Probabilities: Historical seasons are stratified into equal thirds based on 1991–2020 climatology: Wetter (top 33.3%), Near-normal (middle 33.3%), and Drier (bottom 33.3%). Under random chance or neutral ocean conditions, each tercile has an unconditional base rate of ~33%. Shifts away from 33% quantify the empirical teleconnection strength.
Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)
Why this data & analysis? Non-Parametric Teleconnection Evidence

Honest Physical Limits: Standard linear correlation models oversimplify East African climate teleconnections because rainfall responses are asymmetric and non-linear. The empirical contingency matrix stratifies the historical 44-year record into discrete ocean driver intensity bands (Strong, Moderate, Neutral/Weak) and computes the exact empirical tercile distribution (Wetter / Near-normal / Drier) for each state. This gives planners non-parametric, physically transparent probabilities directly matching KMD 3-tier seasonal forecasts.

Key Assumptions
  • Tercile Climatological Equal-Likelihood: Under climatology, each tercile (Wet, Near, Dry) has an unconditional base rate of 33.3% over the 1991–2020 normal period.
  • Small-Sample Transparency: Groups with fewer than 4 historical seasons are explicitly flagged with an asterisk (*) to warn against interpreting isolated anecdotes as statistical proof.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Sample Size Constraints: Super El Niño and Super +IOD events are rare extremes (n = 3–5 events in 44 years), limiting sample sizes for extreme composite bins.
  • MAM Driver Independence: The Western-V gradient partially decouples from equatorial Pacific ENSO during the Long Rains (MAM), reflecting subtropical Western North Pacific wave trains.
Primary Source: NOAA CPC ONI • HadISST / ERSST DMI • CHIRPS v3 Terciles • s3://digital-atlas/domain=climate/type=indices/
Figure 3.3

How Strongly Do Equatorial Ocean Temperatures Govern County Rainfall?

Candidate ocean driver comparison table, continuous bivariate scatter distribution, and linear regression across all 44 historical seasons (1981–2024).

Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)
Why this data & analysis? Continuous Teleconnection Sensitivity

Bridging Discrete Bins to Continuous Sensitivity: While contingency matrices (Figure 3.2) group ocean drivers into coarse categorical bins, climate finance proposal writers and disaster contingency planners require exact marginal response metrics: for every +0.5°C or +1.0°C rise in equatorial Pacific SST (RONI) or Western Indian Ocean SST (DMI), how many additional millimetres or percentage points of rainfall are expected? This continuous scatter plot and ordinary least squares (OLS) regression line across all 44 historical years (1981–2024) provides the empirical slope, Pearson correlation coefficient (r), coefficient of determination (R²), and two-tailed p-value.

Key Assumptions
  • Climatological Normal: Anomalies are computed against the WMO standard 1991–2020 reference period.
  • Linear Bivariate Modeling: OLS regression provides the linear teleconnection slope. Non-linear saturation effects during super-events (e.g. 1997, 2023) are visible as residual scatters from the trendline.
  • Seasonal Alignment: OND rainfall is paired with OND ocean indices; MAM rainfall is paired with MAM ocean indices (Western-V / WNP).
Caveats & Statistical Power
  • Collinearity: ENSO and the Indian Ocean Dipole often co-occur during OND (e.g. positive IOD + El Niño in 1997, 2006, and 2023, or standalone extreme +IOD during neutral ENSO in 2019). Raw bivariate r reflects combined ocean basin influence; check the candidate table for multi-driver variance.
  • Outlier Leverage: Extreme years like 1997 and 2023 exert leverage on the slope; points are explicitly labeled to inspect leverage.
Primary Sources: NOAA CPC ONI • HadISST DMI • CHIRPS v3 • data/KE-enso-explorer/chirps_county.parquet
3 Historical Climate Evidence • 3.2 Climate Maps

Section 3.2 • Gridded Satellite Climate History & Flood Diagnostics — Marsabit

High-resolution pixel-by-pixel spatial raster maps across historical seasons and hydrodynamic flood exposure benchmarks.

Figure 3.4

Multi-Decadal Gridded Field History & Spatial Patterns (Per-Year Field Canvas Grid)

High-resolution pixel-by-pixel spatial raster maps (CHIRPS v3, SPEI-3, MODIS NDVI, Copernicus GFM Flood, FEWS WRSI) across historical years, tinted by ocean teleconnection state.

Why Pixel-by-Pixel Verification Matters: County-level spatial averages mask extreme local gradients across Kenya's complex topography. By inspecting per-year gridded rasters across independent earth observation systems (CHIRPS v3 rainfall, SPEI-3 drought index, MODIS NDVI vegetation health, Copernicus GFM SAR satellite flood extent, and FEWS/USGS WRSI crop-water satisfaction), proposal teams and disaster managers can verify whether a regional teleconnection anomaly (e.g. 1997 or 2023 El Niño) penetrated into specific pastoral subcounties, grazing corridors, or highland agricultural zones.
Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)
Module A: Plot Capabilities & Visual Interpretation
  • Per-Year Facet Canvas: Renders 40+ years of high-resolution gridded satellite observations in an interactive multi-column grid, clipped to official IEBC county boundaries.
  • Ocean Teleconnection Tint: Each year card is subtly tinted by the standardized anomaly (z-score) of the selected oceanic driver (PRGn diverging palette by default: green for wet teleconnection states, purple for suppressing dry states).
  • Anomaly vs. Climatology: Rainfall displays standardized departure from the WMO 1991–2020 reference normal by default (±300 mm scale), isolating true teleconnection impacts from baseline aridity.
  • Multi-Sensor Diagnostics: Switch between 5 earth observation systems to evaluate whether atmospheric moisture translated into surface drought (SPEI-3), vegetation biomass (NDVI), inundation (GFM), or crop satisfaction (WRSI).
Module B: Assumptions, Limitations & Caveats
  • Reference Climatology Baseline: Rainfall anomalies are computed against 1991–2020 WMO standard normal. SPEI-3 is already standard-normalized; MODIS NDVI and Copernicus GFM do not have 30-year baselines.
  • Copernicus GFM Record Length & SAR Masking: Sentinel-1 SAR flood coverage spans only 2018–2025. It reflects recent flood-proneness and orbital pass timing, NOT long-term return-period magnitude. Value 255 (unobserved swath) is strictly excluded as NoData, never counted as dry.
  • HTTP Range COG Streaming: GeoTIFF rasters are window-read on the fly via HTTP range requests against AWS S3 CloudFront, fetching only the county bounding box to preserve client memory.
Module C: Methods & Analysis Summary
  • Driver Independence (Frisch-Waugh-Lovell): Correlation chips display bivariate Pearson r alongside partial correlation (controlling for other drivers) to eliminate double-counting of collinear ENSO and IOD signals.
  • Multi-Driver Linear Combination: Ordinary least squares (OLS) regression calculates the optimal multi-driver variance explained (adjusted R²), identifying whether joint monitoring beats single indices.
  • Phase Intensity Gating: Categorical intensity presets filter analogue historical seasons at |z| ≥ 1.0σ (moderate) and |z| ≥ 1.5σ (strong/extreme) thresholds.
CDH Master Catalog Records: Authored africa-precipitation-monthly-seasonal • Authored africa-spei-drought • Authored eastafrica-ndvi-modis • Authored kenya-flood-gfm • Authored eastafrica-wrsi-fews
Figure 3.5

Sub-County Flood Inundation & Infrastructure Exposure Explorer

Interactive flood exposure reconciling Copernicus GFM Sentinel-1 SAR satellite observations and EC JRC GloFAS 10- to 500-year hydrodynamic flood return periods.

Why Reconciling Satellite & Hydrodynamic Modeling Matters: While satellite radar (SAR) observes individual historical flood footprints, it cannot establish return-period probabilities before disasters occur. The European Commission Joint Research Centre (EC JRC) Global River Flood Hazard Maps v2.1 dataset provides 90 m hydrodynamic flood inundation modeling (2D LISFLOOD-FP forced by GloFAS v4 runoff, evaluating 10- to 500-year return periods; Baugh et al. 2024). Toggling between observed Copernicus GFM Sentinel-1 SAR footprints (curated across 2018–2025 from Copernicus's January 2015–present archive) and modelled probabilistic benchmarks gives planners a complete picture of contingent vulnerability.
Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)
Module A: Plot Capabilities & Visual Interpretation
  • Dual-Source Diagnostics: Toggle between observed satellite radar footprints (Copernicus GFM Sentinel-1 SAR curated across 2018–2025) and modelled probabilistic benchmarks (EC JRC Global River Flood Hazard Maps v2.1 10- to 500-year return periods).
  • Multi-Scenario Comparison: Select multiple return period checkboxes (10 to 500 years) to compare the non-linear expansion of inundated territory against built infrastructure.
  • Population Denominators: Headcounts reflect official KNBS census levels (2019 Census & 2026 projections), distributed across constituencies using WorldPop 100 m residential building footprints.
Module B: Assumptions, Limitations & Caveats
  • HOT-OSM Volunteer Gaps: Health center and school locations originate from crowdsourced Humanitarian OpenStreetMap (HOT-OSM). In remote pastoral counties, crowdsourced coverage is incomplete. A value of zero exposed schools reflects absence of volunteer mapped points, NOT immunity to floods.
  • Geomorphic Drainage & Flash Floods: GloFAS models riverine overtopping along major river channel networks (e.g., Tana, Athi, Nyando, Ewaso Ng'iro, Daua). However, in arid and semi-arid (ASAL) counties such as Marsabit, drainage is dominated by ephemeral sand-rivers (laggas / wadis) terminating into endorheic basins (Lake Turkana and the Chalbi Desert pan) rather than perennial river networks. Sudden convective cloudbursts flushing through these laggas are not fully captured by continental riverine models. Permanent waterbodies (Lake Turkana) and seasonal salt pans (Chalbi Desert) are masked out (HydroLAKES & RCMRD land cover) to prevent conflating natural water surfaces with flooded assets.
  • Stationarity Assumption: Return periods assume stationary hydrologic extremes over the 1979–2022 reanalysis window; intensifying warming may shift 100-year events into 50-year frequencies.
Module C: Methods & Analysis Summary
  • Hydrodynamic Routing: 2D LISFLOOD-FP hydrodynamic modeling (EC JRC Global River Flood Hazard Maps v2.1, 90 m, forced by GloFAS v4 runoff; Baugh et al. 2024), routing peak discharge across digital elevation models to compute flood water depth rasters for 10- to 500-year return periods.
  • Spatial Exposure Intersect: Performed via DuckDB spatial polygon-in-raster operations, clipping depth surfaces at ≥ 0.15 m threshold across subcounty boundaries.
  • Seasonal Flood Dynamics: Both OND and MAM produce severe riverine and flash flooding across Kenya. While OND flooding is strongly modulated by El Niño and positive IOD basin-wide surges, MAM seasons also generate catastrophic riverine flooding across the Tana, Nyando, and Athi basins (as demonstrated in MAM 2018 and MAM 2024, alongside pluvial flash floods and infrastructure failures).

4 Historical Impacts • Multi-Sector Vulnerability

Section 4 • Historical Impacts & Multi-Sector Vulnerability — Marsabit

Quantifying how Pacific and Indian Ocean warming signals propagate through subnational crop yields, pastoral herd demography, market terms of trade, and hydrodynamic flood exposure.

How to Navigate Historical Impacts & Vulnerability: Causal Attribution vs. Statistical Association

Section 3 established the multi-decadal meteorological patterns of rainfall and drought. Section 4 traces the consequential chain of real-world outcomes across four socioeconomic and biophysical domains:

4 Sector Pathways
1. Bimodal Crop & Livestock Balances

HarvestStat & KNBS NAPR audited series. In Kenya's bimodal system, annual agricultural output combines preceding Short Rains (OND) and concurrent Long Rains (MAM). Livestock herd mortality exhibits a 6–12 month biological lag following severe pasture droughts.

2. Pasture Biomass & Market Terms of Trade

864 dekads of MODIS NDVI track continuous rangeland forage flushes and deficits. FEWS NET market prices evaluate Terms of Trade (ToT): the kilograms of maize purchased by selling 1 medium goat, pinpointing acute economic distress.

3. Hydrodynamic Flood & Asset Exposure

Downstream exposure of populations, road networks, health facilities, schools, and electrical grids intersected with Copernicus GFM Sentinel-1 SAR observed inundation and EC JRC GloFAS return periods.

4. Humanitarian Emergency Chronology

UN OCHA ReliefWeb disaster situation reports (2010–2026). Tracks official flash appeals, disaster declarations, and institutional relief mobilization across historical famine and deluge epochs.

Core Project Guidance — Association is Not Causation: Equatorial ocean indices alter the conditional probability distribution of seasonal rainfall, but local socioeconomic impacts are mediated by soil moisture memory, seed access, animal vaccination, road transport accessibility, and early humanitarian financing. An El Niño warming increases wet-season odds, but realized crop yields depend on agronomic management and pest dynamics.
Figure 4.1

Dual-Season Ocean Drivers vs. Agricultural & Livestock Output — Marsabit

Linking the bimodal climate signal (MAM Long Rains + OND Short Rains) to KNBS county agricultural production statistics and livestock outputs (2016–2024).

The Bimodal Agricultural Attribution Reality: In Kenya's bimodal climate, annual crop production reported by KNBS is the composite result of two distinct seasonal harvests: the MAM Long Rains (planted Mar, harvested Jul/Aug, steered by the Western-V) and the OND Short Rains (planted Oct, harvested Jan/Feb of the following year, steered by IOD and ENSO). Single-season climate shocks can often be absorbed, but consecutive failures across both seasons trigger systemic collapse.
Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)
Why this data & analysis? Official Subnational Series

The "Best Available Data" Reality: Subnational agricultural statistics in Kenya have historically been fragmented. We combine the official KNBS National Agricultural Production Reports (2019–2024) with HarvestStat Africa v1.2 (1965–2024, Lee et al. 2025, Nature Scientific Data) to construct the first continuous, audited multi-decadal production series linked directly to ocean driver indices.

Key Assumptions
  • 5-Year Rolling Climatological Baseline: Harvest anomalies are calculated relative to the preceding 5-year rolling median to account for gradual expansion in cultivated acreage.
  • Lagged Harvest Accounting: OND Short Rains crops are planted in October and harvested in January/February of year t+1; this physical lag is explicitly harmonized in the annual statistics.
Caveats & Limitations
  • ASAL Arid Zone Bias: In Marsabit, rainfed maize is cultivated almost exclusively on high-elevation microclimates (Mt. Marsabit and Moyale bluffs). Rangeland livestock output represents 95% of agricultural asset value.
  • Cross-Edition Discrepancies: KNBS 2023-24 vs 2024-25 editions exhibit slight rebasings (median ratio 0.96); numbers are locked to latest published KNBS revisions.
Primary Sources: KNBS NAPR (2019–2024) • HarvestStat Africa v1.2 • CHIRPS v3 • MODIS MOD13Q1
Figure 4.2

Empirical Ocean Driver Phase Response vs. Mean Output — Marsabit

Evaluating observed range intervals, sample sizes, and average agricultural outputs conditioned on categorical ocean teleconnection states (KNBS audited survey years).

National Harvest-Aligned Attribution Convention: Production years are aligned to the seasons harvested within them: OND of the previous year (t−1) plus MAM of the reporting year (t). KNBS does not publish its own convention; this alignment was selected by testing county maize yields against candidate season mappings (2019–2024). Short-rains drivers (ENSO, IOD) evaluate the state at OND(t−1); Long-rains drivers (Western-V) evaluate at MAM(t).
Note on Eastern Counties: In short-rains dominant counties (Tana River, Meru, Kitui, Makueni), OND of the reporting year (t) is the primary driver (r = 0.40) while MAM is negligible.
Two Rulers, One Field: Figure 4.1 above (KNBS NAPR) and Figure 4.2B below (HarvestStat Africa, compiled by FEWS NET from Kenya Ministry of Agriculture archives) measure the same county with different rulers: different survey vintages, administrative district-to-county rebasings, and revision histories. Read each against its own historical baseline only — never compare an absolute value from KNBS with one from HarvestStat. That is why they are presented as separate figures.
Figure 4.2B

Multi-Decadal Seasonal Crop Harvests & Climate Teleconnections (HarvestStat Africa 1990–2024) — Marsabit

Subnational seasonal crop yields, production, and cultivated area (1990–2024) tied directly to planting-season rainfall terciles. Short Rains crops planted in October are anchored to year t to match OND climate drivers.

Structural Season-Year Anchoring & The Reporting Hole: In HarvestStat, every harvest is anchored to its planting year. Short Rains crops planted in October of year t and harvested in February/March of year t+1 belong to year t — aligning them directly with OND rains and El Niño / +IOD drivers. By default, the recent county era (2015–2024) is displayed; the full record includes a national statistical reporting gap (2002–2014) where subnational seasonal reporting lapsed.
Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)
Why this data & analysis? Harmonized Historical Records

The Longest Subnational Harvest Record: HarvestStat Africa v1.2 (Lee et al. 2025, Nature Scientific Data) digitizes and harmonizes subnational Ministry of Agriculture archives back to 1990. Splitting data into Long and Short Rains allows direct testing of whether wet or dry planting seasons translated into above- or below-normal harvest outcomes over three decades.

Key Assumptions
  • Era-Median Baseline (% of a Usual Year): Anomalies are computed relative to the median of each distinct administrative era (≥7 clean seasons required): 1990–2001 (district-era records remapped to 47 counties) or 2015–2024 (county records).
  • Quality Control Flagging: Upstream QC-flagged observations (flag > 0) are shown with dashed red outlines and excluded from medians and summary statistics.
Caveats & Limitations
  • The 2002–2014 Statistical Gap: Between 2002 and 2014, subnational seasonal crop monitoring was not systematically compiled at county level. This hatched gap represents missing records, not zero production.
  • Different Vintages from KNBS: HarvestStat and KNBS NAPR use different collection protocols and vintages. Absolute levels differ up to 2×; compare only within series.
Primary Sources: Kenya Ministry of Agriculture • FEWS NET Data Warehouse • HarvestStat Africa v1.2 • CHIRPS v3
Figure 4.3

Continuous MODIS Dekadal NDVI Pasture Biomass Dynamics (2002–2026) — Marsabit

Pixel-weighted MODIS NDVI series (864 dekads spanning 2002–2026) across Marsabit County. Values below 100% indicate vegetative drought stress and rangeland forage deficits.

Figure 4.4

Pastoral Market Prices & Terms of Trade (ToT) Monthly Purchasing Power — Marsabit

Monthly retail food and livestock prices monitored across sentinel markets in Marsabit County (FEWS NET Data Warehouse). Evaluating purchasing power collapses during acute drought crises.

Terms of Trade (ToT) Economic Formulation & Temporal Framing: Quantifies pastoral purchasing power as the kilograms of white maize grain purchased by selling one medium live goat:
ToT (kg maize / goat) = Retail Goat Price (KES / head) ÷ Retail Maize Grain Price (KES / kg)
In normal years across Marsabit, 1 goat purchases 60–75 kg of maize grain (2008–2020 climatological baseline median: 63.0 kg/goat). During severe droughts, grazing collapses force distress livestock dumping (depressing goat prices), while grain prices soar. When ToT falls below the 25 kg/goat severe distress threshold, pastoral households experience catastrophic purchasing power collapse.
Methodological Framing Note: The severe >50% purchasing power collapse holds strictly on monthly purchasing power evaluated against trailing 24-month peaks (August 2011: −68.1% to 28.7 kg/goat; October 2022: −65.4% to 33.4 kg/goat; February 2023: −68.1% to 25.1 kg/goat across the full 2020–23 multi-season failure). Annual mean aggregation dampens these crisis troughs (2011: −32.5%; 2022: −37.6%) and masks acute seasonal distress. In addition, 2020 carries only 9 paired months in the sentinel series.

Why this data & analysis? Causal Transmission Mechanism

The "Best Available Data" Reality: Meteorological drought does not directly starve people; the market terms of trade do. The FEWS NET Data Warehouse (USAID) provides monthly retail and wholesale price monitoring across sentinel markets in 42 counties (2000–2026). This connects oceanic temperature anomalies directly to pastoral household purchasing power and acute hunger.

Key Assumptions
  • Mandatory Detrending: Nominal Kenyan Shilling prices are deflated using national CPI and detrended to isolate climate shock spikes.
  • Terms-of-Trade (ToT) Ratio — derived, not sourced: Quantifies the purchasing power of pastoralists as the kilograms of maize grain purchased by the sale of one medium live goat. We compute it here as goat price ÷ maize price from the FEWS NET series; no agency publishes it. Being a ratio, a fall can mean either cheaper livestock or dearer grain — opposite implications for a herder — so read it alongside the two price legs above, never alone.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Sentinel Market Bias: Prices are recorded in primary subcounty hubs (Marsabit Town, Moyale, North Horr); remote nomadic camps face substantial unrecorded transport markups.
  • Cross-Border Trade Flows: Unofficial livestock inflows from southern Ethiopia during regional crises can depress local livestock prices independently of Marsabit rainfall.
  • Food Insecurity Benchmark & Licence (CC-BY-NC-SA-3.0-IGO): Official IPC acute food insecurity phases (Phases 1–5) and humanitarian caseload numbers are published by the IPC Global Support Unit and Kenya Food Security Steering Group (KFSSG). In accordance with CC-BY-NC-SA-3.0-IGO, IPC data are presented strictly for non-commercial reference and cited verbatim; they are never blended or merged into CC-BY-4.0 derived analytical layers.
Primary Sources: FEWS NET Data Warehouse retail prices • MODIS MOD13Q1 • IPC Acute Food Insecurity (CC-BY-NC-SA-3.0-IGO). Terms of Trade derived here from the FEWS price series.
Figure 4.4B

Regional Cross-Border Food Trade Flows & Market Shock Absorber (FEWS NET XBT)

Tracking formal and informal regional grain inflows (Uganda, Tanzania, Ethiopia) buffering domestic market supply and capping price surges during drought years (2010–2024).

The Regional Food Trade Shock Absorber: While local agro-pastoral communities experience severe harvest and pasture contractions during acute drought years, Kenya's food balance is deeply integrated into the wider East African trade basin. Surplus cereal producers in eastern Uganda (moving via Busia and Malaba) and southern Tanzania (moving via Namanga and Isebania) supply hundreds of thousands of tonnes of white maize grain and mixed beans, stabilizing physical market availability and preventing famine-level price spiraling. For northern ASAL counties like Marsabit, the Moyale border post serves as a vital bilateral livestock and grain exchange corridor with southern Ethiopia.
Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)
Why this data & analysis? Regional Market Balance

The "Whole-of-System" Trade Reality: Drought does not respect administrative borders, but neither do regional food markets. The FEWS NET East Africa Cross-Border Trade (XBT) monitoring system tracks formal and informal commodity movements across 34 border crossing points throughout the Greater Horn of Africa (2010–2024). Measuring these trade flows reveals how regional spatial variability in rainfall buffers national food availability when Kenya experiences widespread Long or Short Rains failures.

Key Assumptions
  • Informal Trade Enumeration: In addition to customs declarations, trained FEWS NET border monitors observe informal cross-border movements (head loads, bicycles, handcarts, unmonitored trucks) to capture unrecorded trade.
  • Bilateral Kenya-Touching Flows: Includes all registered commodity flows where Kenya is the destination (Import) or country of origin (Export). Transit trade through Kenya to third countries is excluded.
Caveats & Limitations
  • National Resolution: XBT records transactions at national border points (Namanga, Busia, Malaba, Moyale, Taveta), not destination county markets. Flows represent national market buffer capacity.
  • Price & Policy Distortions: Trade volumes are shaped by export bans, regional import tariffs, currency fluctuations, and nontariff trade barriers as well as agro-climatic deficits.
Primary Source: FEWS NET East Africa Cross-Border Trade (XBT) Monitoring • FAO GAUL 2024 • IEBC COD-AB Boundaries

Why this data & analysis? Operational Radar Physics

The "Best Available Data" Reality: Optical satellite sensors are completely blinded by heavy convective storm clouds during flood crises. Copernicus GFM Sentinel-1 SAR is the sole operational sensor emitting microwave radar pulses to penetrate cloud cover and map open water at ~111 m. Intersecting with official KNBS Census counts and projections distributed by WorldPop 100m building footprint shares provides the ground-truth count of exposed populations.

Key Assumptions
  • Census-Anchored Spatial Distribution: Population totals are calibrated to official KNBS census levels (and annual projections for post-2020 events), distributed proportionally across constituencies using WorldPop 100 m building footprints.
  • Year-Matched Denominators: Observed flood events are matched against the population denominator of their respective flood year (multi-year sums mix population vintages).
  • Maximum Seasonal Footprint: Observed extents represent the seasonal composite union of all inundation detected across Sentinel-1 orbital passes.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Orbital Revisit Gaps (Blank ≠ Zero): Sentinel-1 revisit interval is 6–12 days; flash floods cresting and draining within 24h between passes are not recorded.
  • Radar Mask Value 255: Denotes unobserved radar shadow or permanent water—never dry land.
Primary Source: Copernicus GFM Sentinel-1 SAR • KNBS Census Level & Projections (WorldPop 100m share) • s3://digital-atlas/domain=exposure/type=intersect/region=kenya/processing=analysis-ready/
