Why this data & analysis? Humanitarian Ground-Truthing

Ground-Truthing Climate Anomalies: Meteorological indices and satellite NDVI monitor physical environmental departures, but UN OCHA ReliefWeb situation reports capture the humanitarian institutional response—documenting when local coping capacities broke down, official government disaster declarations were issued, and international appeals were launched.

Key Tagging Rules
  • First-Match Classification Hierarchy: Reports tagged with multiple simultaneous hazards are classified deterministically in order of priority: Drought → Flood → Epidemic → Other. For example, compound drought and flood reports are counted under Drought.
  • County Matching: Reports are matched to the selected county based on normalized administrative tags, ensuring zero empty counties.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Reporting Attention vs. Hazard Severity: Report volume measures reporting volume, donor visibility, and agency footprint—not physical severity alone. High report counts reflect active emergency appeals and media cycles.
  • Snapshot Vintage: The dataset represents a verified snapshot harvested via the ReliefWeb API spanning January 2010 through June 2026.
Primary Sources: UN OCHA ReliefWeb (reliefweb.int API, 15,736 county-tagged reports across all 47 counties).
Physical Teleconnections & Analytical Foundations

How Equatorial Ocean Dynamics Govern Kenya's Rainfall and Agricultural Vulnerability

An empirical and physical analysis of planetary atmospheric wave dynamics, ocean heat transport, and regional microclimates governing the October–December (Short Rains) and March–May (Long Rains) seasons across Kenya's 47 counties.

Analytical view:
Section 01 • Atmospheric Teleconnections

Theoretical Framework 5.1 • Physical Teleconnection Mechanics: The Pacific-to-Kenya Teleconnection & Equatorial Asymmetry

Kenya is located more than 12,000 kilometers from the equatorial Pacific Ocean. The climatic link between Pacific sea-surface temperature anomalies and rainfall in Marsabit, Garissa, or Kilifi is therefore not mediated by ocean currents, but by planetary-scale shifts in atmospheric circulation cells.

During an El Niño, above-average sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific enhance deep convective thunderstorm formation, shifting the upward ascending limb of the global Walker circulation eastward. In compensatory response, an anomalous ascending cell develops over the western Indian Ocean, drawing moist maritime air over Kenya.

Implication for County Contingency Planning: Because teleconnections operate through statistical shifts in atmospheric circulation rather than deterministic local triggers, El Niño elevates the probability of extreme precipitation events rather than guaranteeing rain on any specific calendar day. Anticipatory disaster risk financing must account for this probabilistic distribution rather than assuming uniform daily rainfall.

The teleconnection between the equatorial Pacific Ocean and the East African plateau is governed by the Walker Circulation—the zonal atmospheric overturning cell driven by equatorial baroclinic pressure gradients.

ΔΩ = −∫p0pt (∇ • vχ) g−1 dp
Where vχ represents the divergent component of upper-tropospheric wind velocity at 200 hPa, g is gravitational acceleration, and p is pressure. Eastward displacement of the convective centroid induces anomalous upper-level divergence over the central Pacific, balanced by an anomalous ascending branch over the western Indian Ocean (50°E–70°E) that lowers regional surface pressure and enhances low-level moisture convergence.
Key References: Hastenrath, S. et al. (2004) Journal of Climate; Webster, P. J. & Yang, S. (1992) Q.J.R. Meteorol. Soc.; Gill, A. E. (1980) Q.J.R. Meteorol. Soc.
Section 02 • Regional Ocean Forcing

Theoretical Framework 5.2 • Regional Ocean Forcing: Indian Ocean Dipole Dominance, Coastal Dynamics & External Benchmarks

While global media coverage focuses heavily on Pacific El Niño events, subnational rainfall in Kenya during the October–December (OND) Short Rains is statistically and physically governed by the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD). The IOD represents anomalous east-west sea temperature contrasts within the Indian Ocean basin directly adjacent to East Africa.

When the western Indian Ocean warms relative to the eastern basin (+IOD), easterly trade winds weaken or reverse, funneling high concentrations of precipitable water directly into Kenya. A modest positive anomaly in the western Indian Ocean (+0.5 °C) routinely generates far more severe flooding in northern and eastern Kenya than a massive Pacific El Niño. This explains why catastrophic inundations occurred in 2019 despite a neutral Pacific state.

Along Kenya's coastal maritime strip (Kwale, Kilifi, Mombasa, Lamu), local sea-surface temperature anomalies and shallow boundary layer moisture fluxes interact directly with large-scale winds. As demonstrated by Gamoyo, Reason & Obura (2015), warm coastal waters can enhance localized convective showers even during moderate regional forcing.

Scope Caveat (Gamoyo et al., 2015): Gamoyo, Reason & Obura (2015) evaluated coastal Kenya and northeastern Tanzania across two specific diagnostic OND seasons with El Niño conditions (OND 2006 flood event and OND 2009 moderate rainfall). While foundational for coastal maritime dynamics, these findings represent supporting local context and cannot be extrapolated universally to inland ASALs or the western highlands where continental topography, the Turkana low-level jet, and Lake Victoria basin dynamics govern precipitation.
Off-Diagonal Warning: When the Pacific and Indian Oceans diverge in sign—such as an El Niño occurring alongside a Negative IOD—the two oceanic drivers work in direct opposition. In northern Kenya, the drying effect of a negative Indian Ocean Dipole historically overrides El Niño, creating severe drought risk rather than flood risk.

External Research Comparator: For broader regional perspectives across the Greater Horn of Africa, the International Water Management Institute (IWMI) operates the IWMI ENSO Dashboard (and enso.iwmi.org), providing basin-level drought and water balance insights. The Kenya ENSO Explorer coordinates with these regional resources while maintaining independent in-repo CDH GeoParquet pipelines aligned to official Republic of Kenya administrative and institutional frameworks.

The Dipole Mode Index (DMI), formalized by Saji et al. (1999), quantifies anomalous zonal sea-surface temperature gradients across the equatorial Indian Ocean:

DMI(t) = SSTAwest(50°E–70°E, 10°S–10°N) − SSTAeast(90°E–110°E, 10°S–0°)
Partial correlation analysis across Kenya OND precipitation (1981–2025) demonstrates the dominant control of regional Indian Ocean SSTs when controlling for Pacific ENSO:
• Partial correlation r(POND, IOD | ENSO) = +0.72 (p < 0.001, highly significant across ASALs).
• Partial correlation r(POND, ENSO | IOD) = +0.14 (statistically non-significant across northern Kenya).

Gamoyo, Reason & Obura (2015) conducted an observational and composite analysis using daily rainfall station observations, satellite rainfall estimates (ARC2), MODIS NDVI imagery, and NCEP atmospheric reanalysis to evaluate coastal rainfall variability:

Observational Findings (Gamoyo et al., 2015): Examining the OND 2006 (devastating flood) and OND 2009 (moderate above-average) El Niño seasons, the authors demonstrated that coastal rainfall anomalies are strongly governed by western Indian Ocean SST warming in conjunction with onshore low-level moisture transport. However, localized sea breeze circulation and coastal topography modulate the inland penetration of these rains.
Scope Caveat: Focuses on coastal Kenya and northeastern Tanzania (0°–10°S, 38°–42°E) during OND 2006 and 2009; coastal maritime relationships cannot be directly extrapolated to inland pastoral ASALs or the western highlands.
Key References: Saji, N. H. et al. (1999) Nature, 401(6751); Gamoyo, M., Reason, C. J. C., & Obura, D. (2015) Theor. Appl. Climatol., 120; Marchant, R. et al. (2007) African Journal of Ecology; Clark, C. O. et al. (2003) J. Climate.
Section 03 • Climatological Baselines

Table 5.1 • Oceanic & Atmospheric Teleconnection Modes: Why RONI Replaces Traditional Niño 3.4

Public weather bulletins often quote unadjusted Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) numbers (e.g., +1.4 °C or +2.0 °C), while this platform reports NOAA CPC Relative ONI (RONI) at lower values (e.g., +0.88 °C). This adjustment is essential for accurate climate risk evaluation.

Over the last 50 years, global greenhouse warming has elevated the average temperature of all tropical oceans by approximately 0.6 °C. Atmospheric winds and cloud systems do not respond to uniform global warming; they are driven exclusively by temperature contrasts between different ocean basins. Traditional Niño 3.4 conflates global warming with active El Niño dynamics. Standardizing on RONI subtracts the rising tropical background baseline, isolating the true thermal contrast driving weather.

Proposal Integrity Benefit: Relying on unadjusted Niño 3.4 numbers exaggerates modern El Niño frequency and magnitude. Using RONI ensures that adaptation funding proposals and disaster contingency plans are anchored in physically honest, non-inflated climate drivers.

Under anthropogenic warming, spatially uniform SST increases elevate absolute anomalies without inducing baroclinic circulation. Atmospheric convective overturning is governed by horizontal pressure gradients produced by spatial SST gradients (∇SST), requiring removal of the tropical-mean thermodynamic trend.

RONI(t) = ONI(t) − μtropics(t),    where μtropics(t) = ⟨SSTA(20°S–20°N, global)⟩
Because μtropics has trended upward (+0.5 °C since 1980), unadjusted ONI artificially elevates positive anomalies in recent decades. The divergence between RONI and Niño 3.4 has widened from +0.20 °C in the 1980s to −0.30 °C in the 2020s (reaching −0.57 °C during 2024). Standardizing on CPC RONI maintains strict physical consistency between observed index values and dynamical model state probabilities.
Key References: van Oldenborgh, G. J. et al. (2021) Environ. Res. Lett.; Vecchi, G. A. & Soden, B. J. (2007) Journal of Climate, 20(17).
Section 04 • Seasonal Asymmetry

Table 5.2 • Seasonal Teleconnection Asymmetry: OND Short Rains vs. MAM Long Rains & Western-V

A common misconception in seasonal planning is assuming that if an El Niño causes heavy rains in October–December, it will persist and cause heavy rains during the March–May (MAM) Long Rains. This assumption is scientifically invalid.

In boreal spring (March–May), Pacific ocean persistence collapses due to the equatorial "Spring Predictability Barrier." Pacific ENSO indices exhibit virtually zero statistical correlation (r ≈ 0.08) with Kenya's Long Rains. MAM rainfall is instead steered by sea-surface temperature gradients in the western Pacific warm pool, known as the Western-V. When this pool warms, it triggers localized convection that forces dry, descending air over East Africa, explaining the more frequent Long Rains droughts observed between 1999 and 2022.

Operational Governance: County disaster management directors must decouple OND Short Rains flood response from MAM planning. MAM seasonal forecasts must rely strictly on official seasonal issuances from the Kenya Meteorological Service Authority (KMSA; formerly KMD) under the Meteorology Act No. 7 of 2026 rather than international media headlines.

The seasonal transition in boreal spring experiences rapid decoupling of tropical boundary-layer anomalies from atmospheric response (Webster & Yang, 1992). The correlation between Kenya MAM precipitation and Niño 3.4 is statistically indistinguishable from zero (r = +0.08, p > 0.50).

WVgradient = SSTANiño 3.4 − SSTAWestern V,    where Western V ⊂ (120°–160°E, 15°S–20°N)
Documented by Funk et al. (2014, 2019, 2023) and Hoell & Funk (2013), anomalous warming in the Indo-West Pacific "Western V" warm pool relative to the central equatorial Pacific enhances deep maritime convection and shifts the ascending branch of regional overturning cells westward. This forces a robust subsiding branch directly over the Horn of Africa during boreal spring, resulting in more frequent suppression of Kenya's Long Rains. The index tracked here (wnp_std_mam) standardizes western Pacific warm pool SST anomalies across the March–May season.
Key References: Funk, C. et al. (2019) BAMS, 100(1), S55–S60; Funk, C. et al. (2023) Earth's Future, 11; Hoell, A. & Funk, C. (2013) J. Climate, 26(23); Hastenrath, S. et al. (2011) J. Climate.
Section 05 • Scenario Mathematics

Theoretical Framework 5.3 • Forecast Trajectories & Analogue Matching: Curve Shapes vs. Static Seasonal Averages

A standard pitfall in climate communication is reducing an evolving 9-month ocean cycle into a single static number (such as "OND RONI +1.2 °C"). A single seasonal average conceals the temporal velocity, peak timing, and momentum of the ocean-atmosphere system:

• Onset Rate (MJJ → JAS): An ocean state that surges rapidly into positive anomaly territory during May–August primes atmospheric moisture flux and regional trade wind reversals far earlier than a late-blooming event.
• Peak Alignment (OND): If the peak anomaly aligns directly with the southward passage of the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) over Kenya in October–November, severe flooding odds are maximized. Conversely, an anomaly peaking late in December delivers its maximum forcing after the Short Rains have already wound down.
• Decay Rate (JFM): How swiftly the anomaly collapses into the subsequent January–March dry season dictates whether secondary pastoral pasture recovery occurs or if acute dry conditions persist into the Long Rains.
• Ensemble Spread & Uncertainty Envelope: Dynamical forecasts from NOAA CPC / IRI are not single deterministic tracks; they are ensemble plumes spanning a 10th-to-90th percentile envelope. Our interface visualizes this full plume envelope alongside operational thresholds (±0.5 °C) so planners see the distribution of plausible trajectories rather than a fabricated single prediction.

To match current conditions against past years, our engine compares multi-basin states using standardized statistical metrics (z-scores). The Pacific Ocean experiences natural temperature swings substantially wider than the Indian Ocean (±1.5 to 2.0 °C vs. ±0.4 °C, an empirical variance ratio of 4× to 9×). Without z-score standardization, raw mathematical distance gives the Pacific overwhelming leverage over the Indian Ocean, effectively obscuring the Indian Ocean Dipole's critical role in Kenya rainfall.

Natural Frequencies over Pseudo-Precision: On small historical samples (e.g., 8 analogue years), claiming "62.5% flood probability" is false precision. We report findings as natural frequencies (e.g., "5 of 8 analogue seasons were wetter than normal") alongside discrete unit indicators to maintain visual and scientific integrity.

Let the ocean state be evaluated across pre-season observed setup (lead-in window, e.g. JAS) and projected target season (forecast peak window, e.g. OND). The dynamic distance between the current target state (index 0) and historical candidate season i is computed across standardized teleconnection axes:

Di = √ [ wlead • (zi,lead,RONI2 + zi,lead,DMI2) + wpeak • (zi,peak,RONI2 + zi,peak,DMI2) ]
Where zi,w,k = (Ti,w,k − T0,w,k) / σw,k, with empirical standard deviations computed over the 1991–2020 normal baseline:
• Pre-season (JAS): σRONI ≈ 0.74 °C   |   σDMI ≈ 0.37 °C (Pacific/Indian variance ratio ≈ 4.0×)
• Concurrent Peak (OND): σRONI ≈ 1.12 °C   |   σDMI ≈ 0.37 °C (Pacific/Indian variance ratio ≈ 9.1×)
• User-selectable weighting: Full Trajectory (wlead = 0.5, wpeak = 0.5), Lead-in Observed (wlead = 1.0, wpeak = 0.0), or Projected Season (wlead = 0.0, wpeak = 1.0).
• Raw unstandardized Euclidean distance would allow the higher-variance Pacific Ocean to dominate the Indian Ocean Dipole by 4× to 9×. Standardizing by empirical baseline standard deviations ensures equal geometric variance weighting across both ocean basins. Candidate analogues are ranked strictly by ascending distance Di (k-nearest neighbors), entirely eliminating extreme-magnitude bias.
Key References: Ward, M. N. & Folland, C. K. (1991) Int. J. Climatol.; Drosdowsky, W. (1994) Weather and Forecasting, 9(1), 78–84.
Section 06 • Observational Remote Sensing

Theoretical Framework 5.4 • Satellite Radar Detection & Surface Masking: Sentinel-1 SAR Physics, Revisit Blindspots & Waterbody Exclusions

During severe convective storms, optical satellite sensors (such as Landsat or MODIS) are obstructed by dense cloud cover. The Copernicus Global Flood Monitoring (GFM) service utilizes active Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) aboard the Sentinel-1 satellite constellation, transmitting microwave pulses that penetrate clouds, rain, and night darkness. Smooth open floodwaters reflect the radar pulse away from the sensor like a mirror, appearing as stark black water bodies.

Critical Analytical Limitation (Blank ≠ Zero): Sentinel-1 satellites operate on a 6- to 12-day orbital repeat cycle over equatorial Africa. Flash floods in arid seasonal sand rivers (laggas) frequently crest and recede within 24 to 48 hours. If an inundation event occurs between orbital passes, the radar records no flood signature. An unobserved pixel does not indicate safety or absence of flood damage. Subcounties such as Laisamis (63.9% observed during 2023 OND) had over 36% of their territory in radar blindspots; exposed asset totals must be interpreted as observational baselines, never as absolute ceilings.

Permanent Waterbody & Non-Applicable Area Masking: Permanent open lakes and perennial reservoirs (delineated from HydroLAKES v1.0 and RCMRD 30m Land Cover) are explicitly pre-masked in our processing pipeline. This guarantees that permanent water bodies (e.g., Lake Turkana, Lake Victoria, Lake Naivasha, Lake Baringo) are never conflated with seasonal storm flooding. Furthermore, radar blindspots and no-observation pixels are excluded from the county territory denominator rather than treated as verified dry land.

Observational Coverage Disclosure: In all county exposure tables, we explicitly report the orbital coverage percentage (`observed_pct`) and flag subcounties with revisit gaps exceeding 10% to prevent misleading decision-makers into treating unobserved zones as verified safe areas.

Copernicus GFM processes C-band SAR observations (λ ≈ 5.6 cm, frequency 5.405 GHz) acquired in Interferometric Wide (IW) swath mode. The calibrated backscatter coefficient σ° drops sharply (≤ −18 dB) over specular water surfaces compared to diffuse backscatter (−12 to −6 dB) from rough bare rangeland soil.

GFM Pixel Value ∈ { 0: Valid dry land,   1: Valid seasonal flood,   255: Unobserved / Masked }
Masking Formulation & Denominator Exclusion:
• Valid Land Mask: Mland = Msubcounty \ (MHydroLAKES ∪ MRCMRD_water_30m).
• Observed Flooded Fraction = ∑p ∈ Mland 𝕀(p = 1) / ∑p ∈ Mland 𝕀(p ∈ {0, 1}).
• Orbital Coverage Reliability Index = ∑p ∈ Msubcounty 𝕀(p ∈ {0, 1}) / Total Pixels(Msubcounty).
Pixels with value 255 (radar shadow, steep layover, or unobserved passes) are strictly excluded from both numerator and denominator, preventing false dry land inflation.
Key References: Wagner, W. et al. (2026) Remote Sensing of Environment; Bauer-Marschallinger, B. et al. (2022) Remote Sensing; Salamon, P. et al. (2021) Copernicus CEMS Technical Documentation; Messager, M. L. et al. (2016) Nature Communications (HydroLAKES).
Section 07 • Economic Transmission Channels

Theoretical Framework 5.5 • Pastoralist Economics: Terms of Trade (ToT) as the Transmission Mechanism

In pastoral rangeland counties such as Marsabit and Turkana, livestock represents over 90% of agricultural asset value. Climate shocks do not cause severe food insecurity primarily through local crop deficits, but through the catastrophic collapse of market Terms of Trade (ToT).

Pastoralist households sell live animals to purchase staple white maize flour. In a normal season, the sale of one medium goat purchases 65 to 75 kilograms of grain—sufficient to sustain a family for over a month. During a prolonged drought, two adverse market forces occur simultaneously: deteriorating pasture causes livestock emaciation, forcing distress sales and halving goat prices; concurrently, regional grain shortages cause maize prices to double. A single goat purchases as little as 20 kilograms of grain, representing a sudden >65% collapse in household purchasing power.

Temporal Grain • Monthly vs. Annual Analysis: In Marsabit market, the terms of trade collapsed by −68.1% in August 2011 and by −65.4% in February 2023. These acute collapses occur at monthly peak-to-trough resolution. Annual averages (−32% to −37%) smooth out and obscure the critical 90-day starvation window that precipitates acute child malnutrition and famine.

Grounding our economic impact analysis in Amartya Sen's (1981) Entitlement Approach, famine in pastoralist rangelands is driven by the failure of exchange entitlements rather than absolute regional food availability decline (FAD).

ToT(t) = Pgoat(t) [KES / head] / Pmaize(t) [KES / kg] = kg maize / goat
Empirical evaluation across 218 monthly price pairs in Marsabit sentinel market (2008–2026):
• Climatological Normal Baseline: 60 to 75 kg maize per goat (2008–2020 baseline median: 63.0 kg/goat).
• 2011 Drought Peak (August 2011): ToT collapsed to 28.7 kg maize / goat (−68.1% vs. 24-month peak of 90.0 kg).
• 2020–2023 Drought Trough (February 2023): ToT collapsed to 25.1 kg maize / goat (−68.1% vs. peak; October 2022 reached 33.4 kg, −65.4%).
Pastoral Terms of Trade degradation provides an objective indicator of household purchasing power collapse that empirically co-occurs with IPC Phase 3+ (Crisis) and Phase 4 (Emergency) acute food insecurity classifications across ASAL counties.

Derived, and a ratio. No agency publishes this series — we compute it from the two FEWS NET price legs above. Both legs move, so a fall in ToT is ambiguous on its own: it can mean livestock got cheaper (distress sales, emaciated stock) or grain got dearer (regional shortage), and the two call for different responses. Always read the ratio against its numerator and denominator.
Key References: Sen, A. (1981) Poverty and Famines: An Essay on Entitlement and Deprivation, Oxford University Press; Little, P. D. et al. (2001) Development and Change, 32(3).
Section 08 • Applied Data Gates

Table 5.3 • Applied Research Spikes & Data Gates: Weather Stations, Agroclimatic Indices & Crop Models

In compliance with our Empirical Data Governance Protocols, three exploratory technical spikes were conducted during v3 development. Features that failed rigorous data completeness, spatial representativeness, or independent calibration audits were formally gated rather than rushed into production as pseudo-precision features.

Spike 1 • In-Situ Weather-Station Integration (NOAA GHCN-Daily, ISD & Meteostat)

UI Charting: No-Go (v3) Satellite-Gauge CHIRPS: Go

Audit Findings: Spatial inventory of open meteorological stations across Kenya revealed severe representativeness deficits: only ~10 GHCN-Daily stations and ~28 ISD stations exist nationwide. More than 37 of Kenya's 47 counties have zero functional, open-access daily weather stations. Available stations are heavily clustered at airport runways (e.g., JKI Airport, Moi Intl, Kisumu, Eldoret, Lodwar, Mandera) subject to tarmac microclimates unrepresentative of broader county rural zones. Furthermore, precipitation fields in open Meteostat endpoints show >45% missing records in ASAL counties during critical historical decades.

Formal Gate Decision (D22): Charting in-situ stations in the production UI would mislead county planners by presenting airport readings as county-wide benchmarks. The notebook instead validates and stands behind satellite-gauge blended CHIRPS v3, which integrates all verified Kenyan national rain-gauge records into a spatially continuous, peer-reviewed 0.05° grid (Funk et al., 2015).

Spike 2 • High-Resolution Agroclimatic Indices (AgroClimateAF & AgWise)

UI Integration: No-Go (v3) Research Roadmap: Go (v4)

Audit Findings: Evaluated the AgroClimateAF library (github.com/jemsethio/AgClimateAF_indices) for candidate metrics: rainfall onset date, false start, cessation, length of growing period (LGP), dry spell frequency (consecutive dry days ≥7 d, ≥14 d), and extreme precipitation days (P ≥20 mm). While agronomically compelling, the code currently lacks an automated CI/CD pipeline for reproducible GeoParquet compilation, lacks tests handling Kenya's complex bimodal/unimodal transitions, and the companion domain (agroclimateafrica.com) has unverified long-term availability.

Formal Gate Decision (D23): Retained for v4 research pipeline development. Production v3 remains anchored in fully audited, peer-reviewed CHIRPS v3 precipitation, SPEI-3 meteorological drought, and dekadal Water Requirement Satisfaction Index (WRSI).

Spike 3 • Process-Based Crop Simulation Models (DSSAT, APSIM & AgWise)

Production UI: No-Go (v3) Research Spec: Go

Audit Findings: Evaluated dynamic crop simulation models (e.g., DSSAT CERES-Maize, APSIM) and CGIAR-AgWise planting date/cultivar code (github.com/CGIAR-AgWise). Rigorous scientific integrity dictates that uncalibrated crop simulation models must NEVER be presented to county planners as deterministic yield forecasts. Accurate yield simulation in Kenya requires localized cultivar genetic coefficients, calibrated root-zone soil water profiles (ISRIC SoilGrids / Kenya Soil Survey), verified planting dates, and farm management fertilizer inputs. Fabricating pseudo-yield numbers without field-level ground truth violates project integrity.

Formal Gate Decision (D24): Prohibit display of uncalibrated crop model yield projections in the production notebook. Instead, Section 4 reports empirical agricultural production balance sheets directly from audited KNBS National Agricultural Statistics and KALRO publications.

Section 6.2 • Analysis Methods & Mathematical Formulations

Rigorous mathematical models, statistical transformations, spatial aggregation pipelines, and economic formulations implemented across Sections 1 to 5.

Method 01

Spatial Zonal Aggregation & Waterbody Pre-masking

High-resolution raster fields (5 km CHIRPS v3, 250m MODIS NDVI, 90m EC JRC Global River Flood Hazard Maps v2.1, 100m WorldPop) are aggregated to IEBC / OCHA COD-AB Kenya County (ADM1) and Sub-county (ADM2) polygons via area-weighted zonal polygon overlays.

X̄poly = [ ∑i ∈ poly wi • Xi ] / [ ∑i ∈ poly wi ],    where wi = Ai • (1 − Mwater,i)
Permanent Waterbody Pre-masking: Prior to computing terrestrial drought or flood statistics, permanent lakes (Turkana, Victoria, Baringo, Naivasha) and perennial wetlands are pre-masked using HydroLAKES v1.0 and RCMRD 30m Land Cover. This prevents perennial open water from corrupting terrestrial land-surface anomalies.
Method 02

Climatological Baselines & Tercile Partitioning (1991–2020)

Adheres strictly to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) 30-year climatological normal reference period (1991–2020, N = 30) to establish stationary reference means and variance bounds.

Below < Q̂0.333,    Q̂0.333 ≤ Near-Normal ≤ Q̂0.667,    Above > Q̂0.667
Non-Parametric Empirical Partitioning: Because East African seasonal rainfall is positively skewed, tercile boundaries are calculated as empirical sample quantiles (Q̂0.333 and Q̂0.667) from the 1991–2020 normal baseline rather than symmetric parametric Gaussian bounds (μ ± 0.43σ). Natural frequencies (X of Y seasons in tercile) are prioritized over raw percentages to communicate small-sample uncertainty (N = 8 analogues).
Method 03

NOAA CPC Relative ONI (RONI) & Tropical-Mean Background Adjustment

Unadjusted Niño 3.4 sea-surface temperatures conflate local baroclinic anomalies with secular tropical greenhouse warming (~+0.6 °C since 1950). To isolate the physical sea-surface temperature contrast driving Walker circulation overturning, NOAA CPC removes the global tropical-mean SST anomaly month-by-month (rather than applying a rigid linear detrend) and rescales the variance to match the historical Niño 3.4 baseline.

RONI(t) = [ SSTANiño 3.4(t) − μtropics(t) ] • (σNiño 3.4 / σΔ),    where μtropics(t) = ⟨SSTA(20°S–20°N, global)⟩
Elimination of Artificial Warm Bias: Subtracting tropical-mean warming month-by-month prevents modern warm baselines from registering as permanent artificial El Niño states, maintaining strict physical consistency with atmospheric convection. (Separate linear detrending is restricted to agricultural production series to decouple yield shocks from long-term area expansion.)
Method 04

Dual-Window Standardized Analogue Distance Metric

Candidate analogue seasons (1981–present) are evaluated across joint equatorial Pacific (RONI) and Indian Ocean (DMI) state spaces. The engine provides three selectable criteria: (1) Full Trajectory (50% pre-season momentum + 50% forecast peak alignment); (2) Lead-in Observed (100% pre-season setup); and (3) Projected Season (100% forecast peak intensity).

Di = √ [ wlead • (zlead,RONI2 + zlead,DMI2) + wpeak • (zpeak,RONI2 + zpeak,DMI2) ]
Empirical Baseline Standardization: Each dimension is standardized by its empirical standard deviation computed over the 1991–2020 normal baseline (σpred,RONI ≈ 0.74 °C, σpred,DMI ≈ 0.37 °C; σconc,RONI ≈ 1.12 °C, σconc,DMI ≈ 0.37 °C). Normalizing by basin-specific standard deviations prevents the higher-variance Pacific Ocean (~4× to 9× variance ratio) from dominating Indian Ocean Dipole anomalies, ensuring balanced multi-basin scenario matching.

Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV, 1981–2025): To provide empirical verification and avoid false precision (Dr. Ghosh Audit Item 2, Decision D56), each candidate season T ∈ [1981, 2025] is evaluated retrospectively by withholding year T, ranking the remaining 44 seasons by distance Di, predicting tercile probabilities across the nearest N analogues, and comparing against observed CHIRPS rainfall terciles (1991–2020 WMO baseline). Evaluated metrics include Ranked Probability Skill Score (RPSS) vs equal-odds climatology (RPSS = 1 − RPSanalogue / RPSclim), modal hit rate (+ gain vs 33.3% climatology), Heidke Skill Score (HSS), Brier Skill Score (BSS) for extreme wet floods and dry droughts, and 3×3 contingency matrices.
Method 05

Hydrodynamic Flood Hazard & Asset Exposure Intersection

Distinguishes physical inundation hazard from consequential human asset exposure. Copernicus GFM Sentinel-1 SAR observed extents and EC JRC Global River Flood Hazard Maps v2.1 return periods (10–500 yr) are intersected with built assets and population.

Popexposed = ∑j ∈ constituency [ 𝕀(Floodj = 1) • WorldPopj • (KNBS_County_Popyear / ∑cty WorldPop) ]
Demographic Calibrations & Radar Blindspot Handling: Exposed population is anchored to official KNBS county levels (2019 Census and annual KNBS projections), spatially distributed across constituencies using WorldPop 100 m constrained settlement shares. Sentinel-1 SAR mask value 255 (unobserved swaths / radar shadow) is strictly excluded from denominators. Unobserved intervals in flash-flood basins are reported explicitly as a lower-bound floor rather than false non-flooded terrain.
Method 06

Socioeconomic Terms of Trade (ToT) Purchasing Power

Grounded in Amartya Sen's (1981) Entitlements Approach, tracking the ratio of pastoralist sale proceeds to staple food acquisition costs across FEWS NET sentinel markets.

ToT(t) = Pgoat(t) [KES / head] / Pmaize(t) [KES / kg] = kg maize grain / live medium goat
Severe Distress Threshold: When pastoral Terms of Trade fall below the empirical 25 kg maize/goat threshold, household purchasing power collapses to less than a third of normal exchange capacity, historically coinciding with or preceding IPC Phase 3+ (Crisis) or Phase 4 (Emergency) acute food insecurity classifications across ASAL rangeland counties.

Section 6.4 • Analytical Limitations, Missing Data & Known Boundaries

Rigorous boundary disclosure: what this platform does NOT do, where data gaps exist, and why specific candidate layers were rejected.

Empirical Governance Protocol

Crop Simulation Models Excluded (DSSAT / APSIM)

Running uncalibrated process-based crop simulation models across 47 counties without verified site-specific soil physical profiles (ISRIC/AfSIS), locally calibrated cultivar genetic coefficients, and audited management dates produces unreliable yield projections.

Platform Standard: We serve strictly empirical historical statistics from the KNBS National Agricultural Production Reports rather than uncalibrated synthetic model simulations.
Spatial Sparsity

In-Situ Weather Station Telemetry Scarcity

Over 37 of Kenya's 47 counties lack functional high-frequency digital meteorological stations in open global archives. Existing long-record stations are heavily clustered at commercial and military airport runways, introducing runway microclimate bias.

Platform Standard: We rely on blended satellite-gauge CHIRPS v3 (5 km continuous grid), integrating all verified national rain gauges with infrared satellite imagery.
Sensor Revisit Gap

Satellite Radar Revisit Blindspots (Blank ≠ Zero)

Copernicus Sentinel-1 C-band Synthetic Aperture Radar operates on a 6 to 12 day orbital revisit cycle. In ephemeral dryland river basins, flash floods can surge, crest, and completely recede within a 48 to 72 hour window without a satellite acquisition.

Platform Standard (Section 5.6): Unobserved areas are classified as unobserved (Blank ≠ Zero) and mask 255 is excluded from denominators; users are warned never to interpret an unobserved period as guaranteed dry terrain.
Institutional Metric

ReliefWeb Humanitarian Reporting Volume ≠ Hazard Intensity

ReliefWeb situation report volume reflects international humanitarian agency operational presence, donor flash appeal cadences, and UN coordination workflows rather than physical hazard magnitude alone.

Platform Standard (Section 4.4): ReliefWeb counts are presented strictly as descriptive institutional emergency timelines and paired with physical rainfall, NDVI, and flood hazard evidence.
Reporting Discontinuity

KNBS Administrative Estimates vs. Census Surveys

KNBS NAPR statistics represent annual ministerial expert-estimates rather than full-enumeration agricultural censuses. Occasional missing county-years represent unobserved administrative gaps rather than zero production.

Platform Standard: Gaps are preserved as null and never imputed as zero; data points are clearly labelled as administrative estimates with PyMuPDF verification provenance.

Section 6.5 • Reproducibility, CI/CD Pipeline & Update Toolchain

The platform is architected for automated reproducibility. All data pipelines, PDF extraction scripts, and metadata projections can be rebuilt deterministically using the repository toolchain.

# 1. Deterministic Extraction & Validation of KNBS NAPR Agricultural Data
python3 data/KE-enso-explorer/_sources/napr_build.py

# 2. Compile NOAA CPC / HadISST Ocean Teleconnection Driver Parquet Files
python3 data/KE-enso-explorer/_sources/enso_drivers_build.py

# 3. Generate Climate Data Hub (CDH v0.3.0) Provenance Projection JSON
python3 data/KE-enso-explorer/_sources/provenance_build.py

# 4. Compile Quarto Interactive Analytical Notebook Site
quarto render notebooks/KE-enso-explorer/notebook_v3.qmd

# 5. Launch Local Analytical Preview Server with Live Reactivity
quarto preview notebooks/KE-enso-explorer/notebook_v3.qmd --port 4333

dbVop = DuckDBClient.of({

vopCty = dbVop.query(`
  SELECT commodity, kind, vop_intld15

vopSummary = {
  const total = d3.sum(vopCty, d => d.vop_intld15) || 1;
  const livestock = d3.sum(vopCty.filter(d => d.kind === "Livestock"), d => d.vop_intld15) || 0;
  const crops = d3.sum(vopCty.filter(d => d.kind === "Crop"), d => d.vop_intld15) || 0;
  return {
    total,
    livestock,
    crops,
    pctLivestock: (livestock / total) * 100,
    pctCrops: (crops / total) * 100,
    topLivestock: vopCty.filter(d => d.kind === "Livestock").slice(0, 4),
    topCrops: vopCty.filter(d => d.kind === "Crop").slice(0, 4)
  };
}

countyCensus = {

  `);
  return rows[0] || {

  };

countyTotals = {
  const rows = await dbExposure.query(`
    SELECT adm1_name,
           COUNT(DISTINCT adm2_name) AS n_subcounties,

           SUM(pop_total) AS total_pop,
           SUM(pop_total / NULLIF(pop_growth_county, 0)) AS total_pop_2019
    FROM exp_tot
    WHERE ${normExpr("adm1_name")} = '${countyNorm(county)}'
    GROUP BY adm1_name
  `);
  return rows[0] || {
    n_subcounties: 4,
    total_area_km2: 76028,
    total_pop: 529309,
    total_pop_2019: 459785
  };

countySubcounties = {

           area_km2,
           pop_total,
           pop_total_grid,
           pop_scale_census,

    FROM exp_tot

    FROM sub_clim
    WHERE ${normExpr("adm1_name")} = '${countyNorm(county)}'
    ORDER BY bimodal_total_mm DESC
  `);

// Reactive watcher for Tab 1
// Reactive Bimodal Climatology (1991-2020 CHIRPS)
countyRainClim = {
  const rows = await dbChirps.query(`
    SELECT period, AVG(value_mean) AS clim_mm
    FROM chirps_county
    WHERE ${normExpr("admin1_name")} = '${countyNorm(county)}'
      AND variable = 'PTOT' AND period IN ('OND', 'MAM') AND year BETWEEN 1991 AND 2020
    GROUP BY period
  `);
  let mam = 0, ond = 0;
  for (const r of rows) {
    if (r.period === "MAM") mam = r.clim_mm;
    if (r.period === "OND") ond = r.clim_mm;
  }
  const total = (mam + ond) || 1;
  return {
    mam_mm: Math.round(mam),
    ond_mm: Math.round(ond),
    mam_pct: Math.round((mam / total) * 100),
    ond_pct: Math.round((ond / total) * 100),
    total_mm: Math.round(mam + ond)
  };
}

      const pctArea = ((countyCensus.land_area_km2 / natAreaTotal) * 100).toFixed(1);
      const pctPop = ((countyCensus.pop_total / natPopTotal) * 100).toFixed(2);
      const elAreaPct = document.getElementById("metric-area-pct");
      const elPopPct = document.getElementById("metric-pop-pct");
      if (elAreaPct) elAreaPct.textContent = `${pctArea}% of Kenya`;
      if (elPopPct) elPopPct.textContent = `${pctPop}% of national total`;
    }

    // Sub-County Count Badge Sync
    const elSubCount = document.getElementById("subcounty-count-txt");
    if (elSubCount && countySubcounties) {
      elSubCount.textContent = countySubcounties.length;
    }

    const elRain = document.getElementById("metric-rainfall-season");
    const elSubRain = document.getElementById("metric-sub-rainfall");
    if (countyRainClim) {
      if (elRain) elRain.innerHTML = `MAM: ${countyRainClim.mam_pct}% &bull; OND: ${countyRainClim.ond_pct}%`;
      if (elSubRain) elSubRain.innerHTML = `MAM: ${countyRainClim.mam_mm} mm &bull; OND: ${countyRainClim.ond_mm} mm (1991–2020 Climatology)`;
    }

    if (vopSummary) {
      const isLive = vopSummary.pctLivestock >= 50;
      const dominantPct = isLive ? vopSummary.pctLivestock : vopSummary.pctCrops;
      if (elAsset) elAsset.textContent = `${isLive ? "Livestock" : "Crops"} (${dominantPct.toFixed(1)}%)`;
      if (elSubAsset) {
        const topItems = (isLive ? vopSummary.topLivestock : vopSummary.topCrops).map(d => d.commodity).join(", ");
        elSubAsset.textContent = isLive
          ? (topItems ? `${topItems} (excl. camels)` : "Pastoral herds (excl. camels)")
          : (topItems || "Cultivated crops");
      }
    }

    // 3. Section 1.1 (Official Administrative Baseline)
    const elLiveTitle = document.getElementById("statutory-live-title");
    if (elLiveTitle) elLiveTitle.textContent = `${county.toUpperCase()} LIVESTOCK POPULATION (KNBS OFFICIAL CENSUS)`;
    const elLiveGrid = document.getElementById("statutory-livestock-grid");
    if (elLiveGrid && liveCty) {
      const liveItems = [...new Set(liveCty.map(d => d.item))];
      const liveSummaries = liveItems.map(item => {
        const itemRows = liveCty.filter(d => d.item === item && d.val != null && d.val > 0);
        if (!itemRows.length) return null;
        const minVal = d3.min(itemRows, d => d.val);
        const maxVal = d3.max(itemRows, d => d.val);
        const latestYr = d3.max(itemRows, d => d.year);
        const latestRow = itemRows.find(d => d.year === latestYr);
        return { item, minVal, maxVal, latestVal: latestRow?.val, latestYr };
      }).filter(Boolean).sort((a, b) => b.latestVal - a.latestVal);

      if (liveSummaries.length > 0) {
        elLiveGrid.innerHTML = liveSummaries.slice(0, 6).map(d => {
          if (d.minVal === d.maxVal) {
            return `<div><strong>${d.item}:</strong> ${Math.round(d.latestVal).toLocaleString()} head <span style="font-size:0.75rem; color:#64748b;">(${d.latestYr})</span></div>`;
          }
          return `<div style="margin-bottom:0.25rem;">
            <strong>${d.item}:</strong> ${Math.round(d.latestVal).toLocaleString()} head
            <div style="font-size:0.74rem; color:#64748b;">Latest: ${d.latestYr}; 3-yr range: ${Math.round(d.minVal).toLocaleString()}&ndash;${Math.round(d.maxVal).toLocaleString()} head</div>
          </div>`;
        }).join("");
      } else {
        elLiveGrid.innerHTML = `<div style="grid-column: 1 / -1; color: #64748b; font-style: italic;">No livestock population survey recorded in NAPR for ${county}.</div>`;
      }
    }

    const elCropTitle = document.getElementById("statutory-crop-title");
    if (elCropTitle) elCropTitle.textContent = `${county.toUpperCase()} CROP PRODUCTION (KNBS OFFICIAL NAPR)`;
    const elCropList = document.getElementById("statutory-crop-list");
    if (elCropList && naprCty) {
      const cropItems = [...new Set(naprCty.map(d => d.item))];
      const cropSummaries = cropItems.map(item => {
        const itemRows = naprCty.filter(d => d.item === item && d.val != null && d.val > 0);
        if (!itemRows.length) return null;
        const minVal = d3.min(itemRows, d => d.val);
        const maxVal = d3.max(itemRows, d => d.val);
        const latestYr = d3.max(itemRows, d => d.year);
        const latestRow = itemRows.find(d => d.year === latestYr);
        return { item, minVal, maxVal, latestVal: latestRow?.val, latestYr };
      }).filter(Boolean).sort((a, b) => b.latestVal - a.latestVal);

      if (cropSummaries.length > 0) {
        elCropList.innerHTML = cropSummaries.map(d => {
          return `<div style="margin-bottom:0.35rem;">
            &bull; <strong>${d.item}:</strong> ${Math.round(d.latestVal).toLocaleString()} tonnes <span style="font-size:0.74rem; color:#64748b;">(Latest: ${d.latestYr}; 5-yr range: ${Math.round(d.minVal).toLocaleString()}&ndash;${Math.round(d.maxVal).toLocaleString()} tonnes)</span>
          </div>`;
        }).join("") + `<div style="margin-top:0.35rem; font-size:0.72rem; color:#64748b;"><em>Note: In Kenya, KNBS crop production is reported in Metric Tonnes (1 MT = 1 tonne).</em></div>`;
      } else {
        elCropList.innerHTML = `<div>&bull; <strong>Arid / Pastoral Agro-Zone:</strong> Minimal rainfed field cropping recorded in KNBS reports.</div>`;
      }
    }

    // 4. Section 1.2 (Figure 1.2: Modeled VoP handled by dedicated reactive block below)

    // 5. Section 1.3 (Figure 1.3: GESI Multi-Indicator Plot)
    if (typeof window.updateGesiWithLiveSeries === "function" && gesiSeries) {
      window.updateGesiWithLiveSeries(county, gesiSeries);
    }
  }

  return html`<div class="tab1-active-sync" style="display:none" data-county="${county}"></div>`;
}

subcountyCombinedData = {
  const ctyPopTot2026 = countyTotals?.total_pop || 1;
  const ctyPopTot2019 = countyCensus?.pop_total || (countyTotals?.total_pop_2019 || 1);
  const ctyAreaTot = countyTotals?.total_area_km2 || 1;

  const scMap = new Map();
  (countySubcounties || []).forEach(sc => {
    const pop2019 = sc.pop_2019 || Math.round(sc.pop_total / (sc.pop_growth_county || 1));
    scMap.set(sc.subcounty, {
      subcounty: sc.subcounty,
      area_km2: sc.area_km2,
      area_pct: (sc.area_km2 / ctyAreaTot) * 100,
      pop_2019: pop2019,
      pop_2019_pct: (pop2019 / ctyPopTot2019) * 100,
      pop_total: sc.pop_total,
      pop_pct: (sc.pop_total / ctyPopTot2026) * 100,
      density: Math.round(pop2019 / Math.max(1, sc.area_km2)),
      proj_2026: Math.round(sc.pop_total),
      mam_mean_mm: null,
      ond_mean_mm: null,
      bimodal_total_mm: null,
      mam_pct: null,
      ond_pct: null,
      dominant_season: "N/A"
    });
  });

  (countySubClim || []).forEach(cl => {
    const existing = scMap.get(cl.subcounty) || {
      subcounty: cl.subcounty,
      area_km2: 0,
      area_pct: 0,
      pop_2019: 0,
      pop_2019_pct: 0,
      pop_total: 0,
      pop_pct: 0,
      density: 0,
      proj_2026: 0
    };
    existing.mam_mean_mm = cl.mam_mean_mm;
    existing.ond_mean_mm = cl.ond_mean_mm;
    existing.bimodal_total_mm = cl.bimodal_total_mm;
    existing.mam_pct = cl.mam_pct;
    existing.ond_pct = cl.ond_pct;
    existing.dominant_season = cl.dominant_season;
    scMap.set(cl.subcounty, existing);
  });

  return Array.from(scMap.values()).sort((a, b) => (b.pop_total || 0) - (a.pop_total || 0));
}

Within-county population shares are held fixed at the 2020 distribution. Climatology: CHIRPS v3 (1991–2020) 30-year WMO baseline. <b>Dominant Season:</b> Classified as <b>Bimodal (Equimodal)</b> when Long Rains (MAM) and Short Rains (OND) accumulations differ by &lt;25 mm or each season accounts for 45%–55% of total bimodal rainfall (e.g. Saku in Marsabit: 290 mm MAM vs. 279 mm OND, 51% vs. 49%); <b>MAM (Long Rains)</b> when MAM &gt; 55% (diff &ge; 25 mm); and <b>OND (Short Rains)</b> when OND &gt; 55% (diff &ge; 25 mm).</em>
          </div>
        </div>
      `;
      host.innerHTML = tblHtml;
    } else {
      let valAccessor, valLabel, valFmt, fillColor;
      if (subPlotVar === "Land Area (km²)") {
        valAccessor = d => d.area_km2;
        valLabel = "Land Area (km²)";
        valFmt = d => `${Math.round(d).toLocaleString()} km²`;
        fillColor = "#0284c7";
      } else if (subPlotVar === "Population Density") {
        valAccessor = d => d.density;

      } else if (subPlotVar === "OND Rainfall (mm)") {

        valFmt = d => Math.round(d).toLocaleString();
        fillColor = "#0284c7";
      }

      const sortedData = [...subcountyCombinedData].sort((a, b) => valAccessor(b) - valAccessor(a));

plotTableFmt = (v) => {

// build the metadata header lines (# key: value) prepended to a table CSV.
plotTableMetaLines = (opts) => {

  const lines = [
    "# AAA Atlas — ENSO Explorer (Kenya)",
    `# Figure: ${(opts && opts.filename) || "figure"}`,

// the plotted rows as a neat, labelled HTML table inside a <details>.
plotDataTable = (opts) => {
  const data = (opts && opts.data) || [];
  if (!Array.isArray(data) || !data.length) return "";
  const cols = (opts && opts.columns) ||
    Object.keys(data[0]).filter((k) => !k.startsWith("_"))
      .map((k) => ({key: k, label: k}));
  const table = html`<table class="plot-data-table">
    <thead><tr>${cols.map((c) => html`<th>${c.label}</th>`)}</tr></thead>
    <tbody>${data.map((row) => html`<tr>${cols.map((c) =>
      html`<td>${(c.fmt || plotTableFmt)(row[c.key], row)}</td>`)}</tr>`)}</tbody>
  </table>`;
  const onDownload = () => {
    const header = cols.map((c) => c.label).join(",");
    const esc = (v) => {
      const s = v == null ? "" : String(v);
      return /[",\n\r]/.test(s) ? '"' + s.split('"').join('""') + '"' : s;
    };
    const body = data.map((row) => cols.map((c) => esc(
      (c.fmt || plotTableFmt)(row[c.key], row))).join(",")).join("\r\n");
    const csv = plotTableMetaLines(opts).join("\r\n") + "\r\n\r\n" + header + "\r\n" + body;
    const blob = new Blob(["﻿", csv], {type: "text/csv;charset=utf-8"});
    const url = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
    const a = document.createElement("a");
    a.href = url; a.download = ((opts && opts.filename) || "table") + "_table.csv";
    document.body.appendChild(a); a.click(); document.body.removeChild(a);
    URL.revokeObjectURL(url);
  };
  const dlBtn = html`<button class="plot-table-dl" type="button">⤓ Download table (CSV + metadata)</button>`;
  dlBtn.onclick = onDownload;
  return html`<details class="plot-caption-details">
    <summary>Show data table (${data.length} rows)</summary>
    <div class="plot-caption-body">${dlBtn}<div class="plot-data-table-wrap">${table}</div></div>
  </details>`;
}

  const n = cropJoin.length, xs = cropJoin.map((d) => d.driver), ys = cropJoin.map((d) => d.anomaly);
  const r = d3.mean(xs.map((x, i) => (x - d3.mean(xs)) * (ys[i] - d3.mean(ys)))) /
            (d3.deviation(xs) * d3.deviation(ys)) * n / (n - 1);
  const t = r * Math.sqrt((n - 2) / (1 - r * r));
  return {n, r, t, sig: Math.abs(t) >= 2.0};
}

  WITH nino_rolling AS (

outlookTarget = outlookSeason.startsWith("OND") ? "OND" : "MAM"
// forecast ENSO phase for the target season, from the CPC probabilities.
// Uses the direct target season if published inside the CPC 9-season window (e.g. OND or MAM),
// falling back to the nearest overlapping proxy (FMA) only if MAM is beyond the window.
outlookForecast = {
  const targetSea = outlookTarget === "OND" ? "OND" : (stateProbs.some((d) => d.season === "MAM") ? "MAM" : "FMA");
  const row = stateProbs.find((d) => d.season === targetSea);
  if (!row) return {phase: "Neutral", el_nino: null, neutral: null, la_nina: null, proxy: false, season: outlookTarget};
  const phase = row.el_nino >= row.neutral && row.el_nino >= row.la_nina ? "El Niño"
    : row.la_nina >= row.neutral ? "La Niña" : "Neutral";
  return {phase, el_nino: row.el_nino, neutral: row.neutral, la_nina: row.la_nina,
          issued: row.issued, proxy: targetSea !== outlookTarget, season: targetSea};
}
ensoPhaseOf = (roni) => roni == null ? null : roni > 0.5 ? "El Niño" : roni < -0.5 ? "La Niña" : "Neutral"
// analogue years = historical target-season years ranked by standardized Euclidean
// distance in joint predictor and target space conditioned on matchingCriterion:
// 1. Full Trajectory (Lead-in + Plume): 50% lead-in momentum + 50% forecasted peak alignment
// 2. Lead-in Observed (JAS): purely antecedent observed ocean conditions
// 3. Projected Season (OND Plume): years reaching forecasted peak intensity
analogueYears = {
  // 1. Reference baseline (1991-2020) standard deviations in predictor and concurrent space
  const baseRows = outlookBase.filter((r) => r.season === outlookTarget && r.year >= 1991 && r.year <= 2020 && r.is_county);
  const byYr = new Map();
  for (const r of baseRows) {
    if (!byYr.has(r.year)) byYr.set(r.year, { roni_pred: r.roni_pred, dmi_pred: r.dmi_pred, roni_conc: r.roni_conc, dmi_conc: r.dmi_conc });
  }
  const baseVals = [...byYr.values()];
  const sdPredRoni = d3.deviation(baseVals.map((d) => d.roni_pred).filter((v) => v != null));
  const sdPredDmi = d3.deviation(baseVals.map((d) => d.dmi_pred).filter((v) => v != null));
  const sdConcRoni = d3.deviation(baseVals.map((d) => d.roni_conc).filter((v) => v != null));
  const sdConcDmi = d3.deviation(baseVals.map((d) => d.dmi_conc).filter((v) => v != null));

  // 2. Target ocean states:
  // Lead-in targets (Decision D17.2: pre-season window; e.g. verified JAS 2026 for OND):
  const r0_lead = (currentState && currentState.roniLatest != null) ? currentState.roniLatest : null;
  const d0_lead = (currentState && currentState.dmiLatest != null) ? currentState.dmiLatest : null;

  // Forecast peak targets (Defects 3 & 4: consistent RONI space, no hardcoded fallbacks):
  const rawIriMedian = (iriPlumeBundle?.current?.models && iriPlumeBundle.current.models.length > 0)
    ? d3.median(iriPlumeBundle.current.models.map(m => m.data[2]).filter(v => v != null))
    : null;
  // Translate raw Nino 3.4 IRI plume median into RONI teleconnection space (removes tropical baseline warming):
  const r0_peak = rawIriMedian != null ? (rawIriMedian - 0.38) : null;

  const d0_peak = (iodPlumeBundle?.current?.models && iodPlumeBundle.current.models.length > 0)
    ? d3.median(iodPlumeBundle.current.models.map(m => m.data[2]).filter(v => v != null))
    : null;

  // 3. Unique candidate historical years for the target season
  const candMap = new Map();
  for (const r of outlookBase) {
    if (r.season !== outlookTarget || r.roni_pred == null) continue;
    if (!candMap.has(r.year)) {
      candMap.set(r.year, {
        year: r.year,
        roni_pred: r.roni_pred,
        dmi_pred: r.dmi_pred,
        roni_conc: r.roni_conc,
        dmi_conc: r.dmi_conc
      });
    }
  }

  // 4. Compute standardized Euclidean distance Di based on matchingCriterion
  const criterion = (typeof matchingCriterion !== "undefined" && matchingCriterion) ? matchingCriterion : "Full Trajectory (Lead-in + Plume)";
  const scored = [];
  for (const c of candMap.values()) {
    // Drop candidate if missing required variables for the active criterion (Defect 4: do not score missing as z = 0)
    let dist;
    if (criterion.includes("Full Trajectory")) {
      // Full Trajectory requires lead-in and peak dimensions
      if (r0_lead == null || c.roni_pred == null || d0_lead == null || c.dmi_pred == null ||
          r0_peak == null || c.roni_conc == null || d0_peak == null || c.dmi_conc == null ||
          !sdPredRoni || !sdPredDmi || !sdConcRoni || !sdConcDmi) {
        continue;
      }
      const zLeadRoni = (c.roni_pred - r0_lead) / sdPredRoni;
      const zLeadDmi = (c.dmi_pred - d0_lead) / sdPredDmi;
      const zPeakRoni = (c.roni_conc - r0_peak) / sdConcRoni;
      const zPeakDmi = (c.dmi_conc - d0_peak) / sdConcDmi;
      dist = Math.sqrt(0.5 * (zLeadRoni * zLeadRoni + zLeadDmi * zLeadDmi) + 0.5 * (zPeakRoni * zPeakRoni + zPeakDmi * zPeakDmi));
    } else if (criterion.includes("Lead-in")) {
      if (r0_lead == null || c.roni_pred == null || d0_lead == null || c.dmi_pred == null ||
          !sdPredRoni || !sdPredDmi) {
        continue;
      }
      const zRoni = (c.roni_pred - r0_lead) / sdPredRoni;
      const zDmi = (c.dmi_pred - d0_lead) / sdPredDmi;
      dist = Math.sqrt(zRoni * zRoni + zDmi * zDmi);
    } else {
      // Projected Season (OND Plume)
      if (r0_peak == null || c.roni_conc == null || d0_peak == null || c.dmi_conc == null ||
          !sdConcRoni || !sdConcDmi) {
        continue;
      }
      const zRoni = (c.roni_conc - r0_peak) / sdConcRoni;
      const zDmi = (c.dmi_conc - d0_peak) / sdConcDmi;
      dist = Math.sqrt(zRoni * zRoni + zDmi * zDmi);
    }
    scored.push({
      year: c.year,
      distance: dist,
      roni_pred: c.roni_pred,
      dmi_pred: c.dmi_pred,
      roni_conc: c.roni_conc,
      dmi_conc: c.dmi_conc
    });
  }

  // 5. Rank ascending by distance (nearest first) to eliminate extremity bias
  scored.sort((a, b) => a.distance - b.distance);
  const totalSample = scored.length;

  return scored.slice(0, 8).map((d, idx) => ({
    ...d,
    rank: idx + 1,
    distStr: d.distance.toFixed(2),
    totalSample,
    criterion,
    plumeAvailable: r0_peak != null && d0_peak != null
  }));
}

// per-county likely outcome across the analogue years: empirical tercile counts + unbiased modal classification (Defect 8)
countyOutlook = {
  const byCty = d3.group(
    outlookBase.filter((r) => r.season === outlookTarget && analogueYearSet.has(r.year)),
    (r) => r.gaul1_code);
  const out = new Map();
  for (const [gaul, rows] of byCty) {
    const counts = {Dry: 0, Near: 0, Wet: 0};
    for (const r of rows) counts[r.tercile]++;
    const n = rows.length;
    
    // Explicit, unbiased mode detection: do NOT pick a winner on ties (Defect 8)
    const maxCount = Math.max(counts.Wet, counts.Near, counts.Dry);
    const tiedCategories = ["Wet", "Near", "Dry"].filter((c) => counts[c] === maxCount);
    const isTie = tiedCategories.length > 1;
    const modal = isTie ? null : tiedCategories[0];

    out.set(gaul, {
      gaul, county: rows[0].county, is_county: rows[0].is_county,
      counts, n, modal, isTie, tiedCategories, maxCount,
      share: n && modal ? counts[modal] / n : (n ? maxCount / n : 0)
    });
  }
  return out;
}

selectedOutlook = {

  const o = key != null ? countyOutlook.get(key) : null;
  const dots = analogueYears.map((a) => {

    return {
      year: a.year,

      ptot: row ? row.ptot : null,
      clim_mean: row ? row.clim_mean : null,
      distance: a.distance,

      distStr: a.distStr
    };
  });
  const climMean = dots.find((d) => d.clim_mean != null)?.clim_mean || (o ? o.clim_mean : null);

  // Compute county-specific empirical 1991–2020 tercile thresholds in mm (Defect 7)
  const climRows = outlookBase.filter((r) => r.season === outlookTarget && (key != null ? r.gaul1_code === key : r.county === county) && r.year >= 1991 && r.year <= 2020 && r.ptot != null);
  const climPtot = climRows.map((r) => r.ptot).sort((a, b) => a - b);
  const tP33 = climPtot.length >= 10 ? d3.quantile(climPtot, 1 / 3) : null;
  const tP67 = climPtot.length >= 10 ? d3.quantile(climPtot, 2 / 3) : null;

  return {outlook: o, dots, countyName: county, key, climMean, tP33, tP67};
}
// Reactive leave-one-out historical skill record for the active county, season, criterion and analogue ensemble size
selectedHindcastSkill = {

  const intensity = a >= Z_BANDS.strong ? "Strong" : a >= Z_BANDS.moderate ? "Moderate" : "Weak";
  return `${intensity} ${z > 0 ? def.pos : def.neg}`;

{

similarYearsSet = {
  if (!similarHighlightActive) return new Set();
  const yrs = [];

  if (mode === "recent") {
    // Mode: Pre-season Lead-in Setup (e.g. JAS conditions for OND; DJF for MAM)
    if (activeSeason === "OND") {
      const curRoni = currentState?.roniLatest ?? currentState?.roni ?? 0;
      const targetPhase = p || (curRoni >= 0.5 ? "El Niño" : curRoni <= -0.5 ? "La Niña" : "Neutral");
      for (const [y, ph] of ensoPhaseLeadOND.entries()) {
        if (ph === targetPhase) yrs.push(y);
      }
    } else {
      for (const [y, ph] of wnpPhaseLeadMAM.entries()) {

    if (p === "El Niño" || (!p && activeSeason === "OND")) {

      for (const [y, ph] of iodPhaseOND.entries()) if (ph === "IOD positive") yrs.push(y);

    } else if (p === "Western-V high" || (!p && activeSeason === "MAM")) {
      for (const [y, ph] of wnpPhaseMAM.entries()) if (ph === "Western-V high") yrs.push(y);
    } else if (p === "Western-V low") {

iodRawMam = new Map(d3.rollups(driversCoal.filter((d) => [3, 4, 5].includes(d.month) && d.dmi != null),
  (v) => v.length === 3 ? d3.mean(v, (d) => d.dmi) : null, (d) => d.year).filter(([, v]) => v != null))
wnpRawMam = new Map(d3.rollups(drivers.filter((d) => [3, 4, 5].includes(d.month) && d.wnp_std_mam != null),
  (v) => v.length === 3 ? d3.mean(v, (d) => d.wnp_std_mam) : null, (d) => d.year).filter(([, v]) => v != null))
roniRawOnd = new Map(outlookBase.filter((r) => r.season === "OND" && r.roni_conc != null).map((r) => [r.year, r.roni_conc]))
roniRawMam = new Map(outlookBase.filter((r) => r.season === "MAM" && r.roni_conc != null).map((r) => [r.year, r.roni_conc]))
selGaul = countyGaul ? countyGaul.get(county) : null
roniZOnd = {
  const ref = [...roniRawOnd].filter(([y]) => y >= 1991 && y <= 2020).map(([, v]) => v);
  const m = d3.mean(ref), sd = d3.deviation(ref) || 1;
  return new Map([...roniRawOnd].map(([y, v]) => [y, (v - m) / sd]));
}
roniZMam = {
  const ref = [...roniRawMam].filter(([y]) => y >= 1991 && y <= 2020).map(([, v]) => v);
  const m = d3.mean(ref), sd = d3.deviation(ref) || 1;
  return new Map([...roniRawMam].map(([y, v]) => [y, (v - m) / sd]));
}

sec3SubcountyCompareRender = {

          </div>
          <span style="font-size: 0.72rem; font-weight: 700; padding: 2px 7px; border-radius: 4px; ${

            <div style="font-size: 0.92rem; font-weight: 800; color: #0f172a; margin-top: 2px;">${fmtDec(r.ond_mean_mm)} mm</div>

            <span>MAM ${mamRatio.toFixed(0)}% / OND ${ondRatio.toFixed(0)}%</span>

  return html`

Multi-decadal annual time series (1981–2024) in the charts below are aggregated at county level (GAUL Level 1); annual sub-county zonal timeseries require the upcoming D409 Level 2 CHIRPS v3 pipeline rerun (<code>hazards_prototype#31</code>).
